old_text: Aside from the gathering problem, our work is also in conjunction with the field of fault tolerance via the assumption of Byzantine faults to which some agents are subjected. First introduced in <cit.>, a Byzantine fault is an arbitrary fault occurring in an unpredictable way during the execution of a protocol. Due to its arbitrary nature, such a fault is considered as the worst fault that can occur. Byzantine faults have been extensively studied for “classical" networks i.e., in which the entities are fixed nodes of the graph (cf., e.g., the book <cit.> or the survey <cit.>). To a lesser extend, the occurrence of Byzantine faults has been also studied in the context of mobile entities evolving in the plane, cf. <cit.>. Prior to our work, gathering in arbitrary graphs in presence of Byzantine agents was considered only in <cit.>. As mentioned in the previous section, it is proven in <cit.> that the minimum number ℳ of good agents that guarantees f-Byzantine gathering is precisely 1 for networks of known size and f+2 for networks of unknown size, provided that the Byzantine agents cannot lie about their labels. The proof that both of these values are enough, under their respective assumptions regarding the knowledge of the network size, relies on algorithms using a mechanism of blacklists that are, informally speaking, lists of labels corresponding to agents having exhibited an “inconsistent" behavior. Of course, in the context of our paper, we cannot use such blacklists as the Byzantine agents can change their labels and in particular steal the identities of good agents.
new_text: Our work relates to fault tolerance through the assumption of Byzantine faults, where arbitrary and unpredictable failures occur during protocol execution. These faults are considered the most severe possible. Extensively studied in classical networks with fixed graph nodes (e.g., <cit.>, <cit.>), Byzantine faults have been less explored in mobile entities in the plane (<cit.>). Prior to this work, gathering in arbitrary graphs with Byzantine agents was studied only in <cit.>. As noted, <cit.> proves that the minimum number ℳ of good agents ensuring f-Byzantine gathering is 1 for networks of known size and f+2 for unknown size, assuming Byzantine agents cannot falsify labels. These bounds are achieved using algorithms with blacklists—lists of labels of agents displaying inconsistent behavior. However, such mechanisms are infeasible here because Byzantine agents can alter labels and impersonate good agents.

old_text: We partition such that the low-degree vertices are assigned to the GPUs. The intuition behind this decision is threefold: first, processing the many low-degree vertices in parallel fits the GPU compute model (i.e., many small computations with insignificant load imbalance); second, the low-degree vertices occupy a small amount of memory (as they are not attached to many edges), a critical issue to the space-constrained GPUs; third, and most importantly, processing the low-degree vertices during the bottom-up steps is the main bottleneck as we have empirically verified. As we argue in the next section, this partitioning solution adds one additional advantage: it makes it easier to decide when to switch to bottom-up processing without communicating between partitions.
new_text: We partition the data such that low-degree vertices are assigned to GPU-based processing units. This design choice is motivated by three interrelated factors. First, the GPU’s architecture is optimized for parallel execution of numerous small, independent tasks, and low-degree vertices align well with this model. Because these vertices require minimal computational effort per unit, their parallel processing incurs negligible load imbalance, allowing efficient utilization of the GPU’s thousands of cores. Second, low-degree vertices consume less memory due to their limited edge connectivity, which is crucial for GPUs that operate under stricter memory constraints compared to CPUs. By dedicating these low-memory workloads to GPUs, we avoid over-subscribing their memory resources, which could otherwise degrade performance. Third, handling low-degree vertices during bottom-up processing has been empirically identified as a critical performance bottleneck in our system. Assigning these vertices to GPUs ensures they are processed concurrently, mitigating this bottleneck. Additionally, this partitioning strategy offers a secondary benefit: it enables localized decision-making for transitioning to bottom-up processing. Since low-degree vertices are confined to a single partition, the system can independently determine the optimal switching point without requiring cross-partition communication, simplifying coordination and reducing overhead.

Most optimization efforts proposed in the literature over the past few decades
have focused either on a single performance bottleneck or a single hardware
platform and are, consequently, neither portable nor provide stable performance
gains even within a single hardware platform. This is one of the reasons why
such optimizations are difficult to be applied in real-life
applications. Another reason concerns the non-negligible runtime overhead that
usually accompanies such optimizations. This overhead may include format
conversion, format parameter tuning, reordering the matrix, etc. If the
numerical solver does not have enough iterations to amortize this cost, the
benefit of applying the optimization may be outweighed. To make matters worse,
one might incur the overhead without any guarantee of a performance
improvement. Based on all the previous observations, we have come to believe
that the next solid step for improving SpMV performance no longer involves
proposing new and expensive optimizations, but applying the plethora of
available optimizations whenever they can be effective, i.e., transforming the
challenge of developing new optimizations to selecting an
  appropriate optimization for the target matrix and architecture. We claim
that a “universal” optimization effort for SpMV is feasible, and, towards this
direction, we propose a methodology to automatically select an efficient
optimization for SpMV, that is both application and architecture aware. Our

new_text: Over the past few decades, most optimization strategies in the literature have targeted either a specific performance bottleneck or a particular hardware platform. As a result, these approaches often lack portability across different systems and fail to deliver consistent performance improvements even on the platform they were designed for. This limitation stems from the fact that hardware architectures and problem characteristics vary widely, making single-target optimizations inherently fragile. These shortcomings are critical for real-world applications, where adaptability and reliability are essential. Furthermore, such optimizations frequently introduce non-trivial runtime overhead. For example, tasks like format conversion, parameter tuning, or matrix reordering—while aimed at boosting performance—can themselves become bottlenecks if not carefully managed. If the solver only requires a few iterations to converge, this overhead may not be amortized, effectively negating any potential gains. Worse still, the cost of these optimizations might be incurred without any assurance of success, especially when the chosen method is mismatched to the problem or hardware. Recognizing these challenges, we argue that the next phase in optimizing SpMV performance should shift from inventing new, specialized techniques to strategically applying existing optimizations in scenarios where they are most effective. This approach reframes the problem: instead of designing novel optimizations, the focus becomes selecting the most appropriate one for a given matrix and architecture. By doing so, a "universal" optimization strategy for SpMV becomes viable. To this end, we propose a methodology that automatically identifies an efficient optimization tailored to both the application context and the underlying hardware, incorporating key design principles such as adaptability, efficiency, and robustness.

Note that DL and UL are decoupled over different μ-mmW RATs in the proposed scheme. The association distance reduction via obtaining more UL BSs is the sole advantage of the scheme. It is thus different from μW single RAT UL/DL decoupling <cit.> that resolves the DL/UL imbalance in transmission power and/or scheduling, of which the both mismatches are negligible under an interference-limited UDN (see Definition 1 and discussion after Remark 2).
new_text: To address the uplink (UL) bottleneck in ultra-dense networks (UDNs), we introduce a novel millimeter-wave (mmW) UL decoupling scheme that allows mmW users to offload UL traffic to existing microwave (μW) base stations (BSs) in addition to their own mmW BSs. This approach decouples UL and downlink (DL) transmissions by enabling them to operate over different radio access technologies (RATs)—specifically, mmW for DL and μW for UL, or vice versa. By providing access to a larger pool of UL-capable BSs, the scheme effectively increases UL network density, thereby reducing the average association distance between users and their serving BSs. This densification directly enhances overall UL rates in UDN environments, where interference is the primary performance constraint rather than transmit power. Importantly, the core advantage of this method lies in the spatial diversity of UL BS resources, which differs from traditional μW single-RAT UL/DL decoupling strategies <cit.> that focus on balancing power asymmetry or scheduling inefficiencies between DL and UL. In UDNs, such imbalances become negligible under interference-limited conditions (as defined in Definition 1 and elaborated after Remark 2), making the proposed μ-mmW cross-RAT decoupling uniquely suited to address the specific challenge of UL capacity saturation.

In this paper we presented a cross-platform methodology for optimizing the SpMV
kernel and establish that, depending on the sparsity pattern of the matrix and
the underlying architecture, a suitable optimization can be selected to improve
SpMV performance. We formulate optimization selection for SpMV as a
classification problem, with each class corresponding to a performance
bottleneck. We first propose a profiling-based classifier, that relies on
benchmarking the input matrix to perform the decision making. We also leverage
machine learning to train Decision Tree and Naive Bayes classifiers that use
comprehensive structural features to perform the classification and rely on the
profiling-based classifier for the training process. Experimental evaluation on
115 sparse matrices and three platforms has demonstrated that our methodology is
very promising, especially for the latest many-core architectures, which
intensify various performance issues of the SpMV kernel.
new_text: In this paper, we present a cross-platform methodology for optimizing the SpMV kernel and establish that, depending on the sparsity pattern of the matrix and the underlying architecture, a suitable optimization can be selected to improve SpMV performance. We formulate optimization selection for SpMV as a classification problem, with each class corresponding to a performance bottleneck. We first propose a profiling-based classifier that relies on benchmarking the input matrix to perform the decision-making. We also leverage machine learning to train Decision Tree and Naive Bayes classifiers that use comprehensive structural features to perform the classification and rely on the profiling-based classifier for the training process. Experimental evaluation on 115 sparse matrices and three platforms has demonstrated that our methodology is very promising, especially for the latest many-core architectures, which intensify various performance issues of the SpMV kernel.

Autonomous trajectory execution. One of the most effective approaches for teaching robots to execute a desired task is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), a technique that develops policies from example state to action mappings <cit.>. In this method, sample trajectories for performing a task is demonstrated by the user. The challenge is to extend these demonstrations to unseen situations. Examples of successful application include autonomous helicopter maneuvers <cit.>, playing table tennis <cit.><cit.>, object manipulation <cit.>, and making coffee <cit.>. To gather enough data for the task learning, some researchers proposed to use cloud-based and crowdsourced data collection techniques  <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>. Such approaches can successfully multiply the training data for manipulation tasks where there is a user-independent solution, but cannot be used to train a robot to adapt to the user's preferences.

The network is unrolled for 50 time steps and at each timestep the loss function is defined as the squared error between the predicted and actual value for each element of the end-effector pose and also its status (1 for open and 0 for close). All the parameters are initialized uniformly between -0.08 to 0.08 following the recommendation by <cit.>. Stochastic gradient descent with mini-batches of size 10 is used to train the network. RMSProp <cit.> with initial learning rate of 0.002 and decay of 0.95-0.99 (based on number of examples) is used to divide the gradients by a running average of their recent magnitude. In order to overcome the exploding gradients problem, the gradients are clipped in the range [-1, 1]. We use 90% of the data for training and keep the remaining 10% for validation.
new_text: The network architecture is trained over 50 unrolled time steps, with a loss function defined at each step. This loss is calculated as the sum of squared errors between predicted and ground-truth values for each component of the end-effector pose (e.g., position and orientation) and its binary status (1 for "open" and 0 for "closed"). To ensure stable training, network parameters are initialized uniformly within the range [-0.08, 0.08], following standard practices for avoiding saturation in early layers. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is employed with mini-batches of size 10, balancing computational efficiency and data coverage. Gradient updates use RMSProp, an adaptive learning rate algorithm, initialized with a rate of 0.002. The algorithm’s decay factor, set between 0.95 and 0.99, adjusts dynamically based on the number of training examples to control the running average of gradient magnitudes. To mitigate the exploding gradients issue—a common problem in recurrent models—gradients are clipped to the range [-1, 1], limiting their impact on parameter updates. The dataset is partitioned into 90% for training and 10% for validation, ensuring sufficient data for model learning while reserving a portion to monitor generalization and prevent overfitting.

old_text: Position of the box inside the shelf. In the pick and place task, the user can place the box in an arbitrary location inside the shelf. It is possible to extract this preference from the recorded data and use it to control this behavior. For this purpose, the end point of each task execution (i.e. when the box is inside the shelf) is considered and the box's position in that moment is extracted. The z element of the position which is in the same direction as the shelf's width is added as an input to the network for all the time steps of that particular task execution. Therefore, during the test by giving an arbitrary z position to that input at each time step, the network should generate a trajectory to reach the desired z position inside the shelf. To evaluate how well the network can generate a trajectory to reach the desired position inside the shelf, we compare the position of the box when the task is accomplished with the desired position.

For this purpose, the endpoint of each task execution (i.e., when the box is within the shelf) is considered, and the box’s position at that point is extracted. The z element of the position, which is aligned with the shelf’s width, is included as an input to the network for all time steps of that particular task execution. Therefore, during testing, by specifying an arbitrary z position in this input at each time step, the network should generate a trajectory to reach the desired z position within the shelf. To evaluate how well the network can generate such a trajectory, we compare the box’s position once the task is completed with the desired position.

The fundamental difference between ICN caching and, for example, web caching is that in ICN caching we have a network of caches that can work together to optimise the performance of the whole network.
Although hierarchical web caching implemented similar networks of caches, each cache was operated by a different real-world entity and attempted to optimise its own performance.
This led to issues like the filtering effect <cit.> where first caches in the hierarchy capture the most popular objects because they attempt to optimise their own performance.
This in turn leads to the following caches to see a request stream with less locality, making their performance suffer.
In the context of web caching where every cache is operated by a different entity, this is reasonable, but in the context of ICN, a single entity controls multiple caches and is able to make them cooperate to optimise the overall performance.
Results in <cit.> show that even a simple randomization of where to cache a particular piece of content has a significant boost of overall performance because it mitigates the filtering effect.
As example, consider Figure <ref>.
In the web caching model, the routers next to the clients would cache the most popular content, but in ICN, it is feasible to have some other routers do that, for example the green routers marked with X.
In other words, <cit.> shows that caches being less greedy in optimising their own performance is beneficial to the whole system.
This implies that when evaluating networks of ICN caches, we need to look at the performance of the whole network instead of optimising performance of individual caches.
new_text: The primary distinction between ICN caching and traditional web caching lies in the coordination among caches: ICN employs a network of caches that collaborate to enhance overall system performance, whereas web caching relies on decentralized hierarchies where each cache independently optimizes its own metrics. In hierarchical web caching, these individual caches are typically managed by distinct entities, often leading to suboptimal outcomes such as the "filtering effect" <cit.>. Here, upstream caches prioritize caching high-demand content to improve their own performance, resulting in downstream caches receiving request streams with reduced locality and diminished efficiency. While this approach is reasonable in web caching scenarios due to the distributed nature of ownership, ICN operates under a centralized control model where a single entity manages multiple caches, enabling coordinated optimization of the entire network. Studies <cit.> demonstrate that even simple strategies, like randomizing content placement across caches, can significantly mitigate the filtering effect and improve system-wide performance. For instance, in Figure <ref>, the web caching model would cache popular content at client-near routers, whereas in ICN, a centralized controller could delegate such caching to less proximal routers (e.g., the green X-marked routers), distributing the load more effectively. This illustrates that <cit.> emphasizes the benefits of caches adopting less self-serving behavior for the system’s collective gain. Consequently, evaluating ICN caching networks requires a focus on holistic performance rather than isolated cache-level optimization.

Typically cache performance has been measured via hit rate, which captures the ratio between cache hits (requests found in the cache) to the total number of requests seen by the cache.
Byte hit rate is its natural extension where every hit is weighted by the size of the object, hence byte hit rate measures the reduction in outgoing traffic from the cache.
As our focus is on traffic reduction, we use byte hit rate in the following.
When we apply byte hit rate as the performance metric, we effectively aggregate the whole network of caches as a single cache and look at its performance.
(Note that since multiple caches may hold a copy of the same object in ICN, such an “aggregate” cache has less storage than the individual caches together; this does not influence the metric.)
Byte hit rate is location-agnostic since it only cares whether there was a hit in any cache; it does not provide any information about where the hit happened.
new_text: Cache performance is traditionally assessed using hit rate, defined as the proportion of cache hits (requests satisfied by the cache) relative to the total number of requests. A refined variant, byte hit rate, assigns weights to each hit based on the object size, thereby quantifying the reduction in outbound traffic achieved by the cache. Given our emphasis on minimizing traffic, we employ byte hit rate as the primary metric. This approach effectively consolidates the entire cache network into a single virtual cache for performance evaluation. Notably, in environments like ICN where multiple caches may redundantly store identical objects, the aggregate cache’s effective capacity is lower than the sum of individual capacities, though this does not impact the metric’s validity. Byte hit rate is inherently location-agnostic, as it focuses only on whether a hit occurred in any cache, without specifying the location of the hit.

Topology of the network is also of high importance in a correct experimental setting.
Research has showed that most realistic networks, including the Internet are scale-free, so a Barabási-Albert model could be used to generate synthetic network topologies.
However, as work in <cit.> shows, real ISP router topologies do not always conform to the scale-free model, so it is also important to experiment with real topologies.
As opposed to request traces, network topologies, both at ISP and AS level, are readily available, so unless the experiment setting requires a network much larger than exists in traces, using a real network topology is preferable to synthetic topologies.

Research has shown that most realistic networks, including the Internet, are scale-free, so a Barabási-Albert model could be used to generate synthetic network topologies. However, as demonstrated in <cit.>, real ISP router topologies do not always conform to the scale-free model, so it is also important to experiment with real topologies. Unlike request traces, network topologies at both the ISP and AS levels are readily available; therefore, unless the experimental setup requires a network significantly larger than those available in traces, using a real network topology is preferable to synthetic ones. Research must consider multiple diverse topologies to eliminate biases introduced by specific topologies from the results.

By construction, the graph Laplacian is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Therefore, it admits an eigendecomposition, with non-negative eigenvalues, Ł = U Λ U^T, where each column of U is one of Ł's eigenvectors, i.e., the graph Fourier modes, and Λ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues corresponding to each of the eigenvectors in U. Our attempt in this work is to cast a similar optimization problem to solve source localization problems on graphs. We do this by modeling the source signals as functions whose domain consists on the nodes of the network. In this context, the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian play a similar role as the Fourier modes on the real line, and the diffusion of the source signals can be modeled as the action of a linear operator which is a function of this graph Laplacian <cit.>. Unlike Candès and Fernandez-Granda, however, we do not assume in general that the diffusion process is known. Rather, we assume it to be given by a parametrized function of the graph Laplacian and attempt to learn this parameter at the same time as the source locations. We note, however, that this simultaneous learning makes the overall optimization problem non-convex and initialization-dependent.
new_text: In this work, we frame a similar optimization problem to solve source localization on graphs by modeling the source signals as functions whose domain corresponds to the nodes in the network. In this context, the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian serve a role analogous to Fourier modes on the real line, as they form an orthonormal basis for representing signals on the graph. By analogy to classical signal processing on continuous domains, the diffusion process can be represented as the action of a linear operator that is a function of the graph Laplacian. Unlike the approach of Candès and Fernandez-Granda, we do not assume prior knowledge of the diffusion process. Instead, we model the diffusion as a parameterized function of the graph Laplacian and simultaneously learn this parameter along with the source locations through a joint optimization process. This simultaneous learning introduces non-convexity into the overall optimization problem, making it sensitive to the choice of initial parameter values.

new_text: Re-entrancy is a critical characteristic of AMR graphs that is non-trivial to handle. To address this, we implemented a test for re-entrancy ("Re-entrancy"), focusing only on edges that point to nodes with multiple incoming edges. This approach cannot be evaluated using Smatch, as the graph no longer forms a single-rooted connected structure. Instead, we compute an F-score on these edges, disregarding variable names and relying solely on concept labels. The reduced set of edges in this context eliminates the need to disambiguate between different AMR nodes sharing the same concept label, thereby making Smatch’s variable alignment step unnecessary.

old_text: The SRA estimations seen in <Ref> represent a loose upper bound on the benchmarks' energy consumption. In most cases these bounds cannot be considered safe for use in mission critical applications. However, our experimental results show a low level of SRA underestimation, less than 4%, and therefore our SRA can still provide valuable guidance to the application programmer, e.g. to determine whether or not an application is likely to exceed an available energy budget. Based on our findings, a small over-provision can be introduced to the system's energy consumption to increase the level of confidence.
new_text: The SRA estimations presented in <Ref> provide approximate upper limits for the energy consumption of the benchmarks evaluated. However, in the majority of scenarios, these estimates lack the precision required to be deemed reliable for deployment in mission-critical systems where energy usage must be strictly controlled. Despite this limitation, our experimental results reveal that the SRA method consistently underestimates actual energy consumption by less than 4%, indicating a high degree of accuracy in most cases. This low margin of error suggests that SRA remains a practical tool for application developers, offering actionable insights—such as whether a given application is likely to surpass a predefined energy budget. To further enhance reliability, our findings advocate for the introduction of a small, calculated over-provision—accounting for the observed 4% underestimation—when determining system energy requirements, thereby improving confidence in the predictions without requiring a complete overhaul of the estimation approach.

The Xcore processor is a deeply embedded processor intended to allow hardware interfaces to be implemented in software. This makes the Xcore well suited to embedded applications requiring
multiple hardware interfaces with real-time responsiveness. Interfaces, such as SPI, I2C and USB, can be written efficiently in C-style software, rather than relying on hardware blocks provided in a System-on-Chip or synthesized onto FPGA. To achieve this, the Xcore is designed to be a time deterministic hardware multi-threaded architecture, that provides inter-thread communication and I/O port control directly in the ISA. Moreover, for energy efficiency the processor is event-driven; busy waiting is avoided in favor of hardware-scheduled idle periods.
new_text: The Xcore processor is a deeply embedded architecture engineered to enable software-based implementation of hardware interfaces, making it ideal for applications requiring multiple, real-time responsive hardware interfaces. Protocols such as SPI, I2C, and USB can be efficiently implemented in C-style software, bypassing the need for dedicated hardware blocks in System-on-Chip (SoC) designs or FPGA synthesis. The Xcore achieves this through a time-deterministic, hardware-multi-threaded architecture, where inter-thread communication and I/O port control are integrated directly into the instruction set architecture (ISA). Furthermore, the processor is optimized for energy efficiency via an event-driven model, prioritizing hardware-scheduled idle states over energy-inefficient busy waiting.

old_text: First, SRA was applied to replicated non-communicating threads. The user can make energy-aware decisions on the number of threads to use, with respect to time and energy estimations retrieved by our analysis. As an example, consider four independent matrix multiplications on four pairs of equally sized matrices (30×30). For all three versions we keep the number of cores, the core voltage and frequency the same and we alter the number of threads. Our analysis shows that the single thread version, `M1`, has an execution time of 4× the time needed to execute one matrix multiplication. However, the two-thread version, `M2`, halves the execution time and, as indicated by both SRA and actual measurements, decreases the energy by 21%, compared to `M1`. The four-thread version, `M3`, halves the execution time again and, as predicted by SRA, the energy consumption is decreased by 40% compared to the two-thread version, `M2`. For the same case, `M3 vs M2`, the actual energy savings are 44%. Although there is a different estimation error between different numbers of active threads, the error range of 5% is small enough to allow comparison between these different versions, by just using the energy estimations of SRA. The measured and the predicted values are strongly correlated and confirm that using more threads increases the power dissipation, but the reduction in execution time saves energy on the platform under investigation.
new_text: SRA was applied to replicated non-communicating threads, enabling energy-aware thread-count decisions based on time and energy estimates. For four independent 30×30 matrix multiplications, cores, voltage, and frequency remained constant while threads varied. The single-thread version (M1) executed four matrix multiplications in 4× the time of one, while the two-thread version (M2) halved execution time and reduced energy by 21% (SRA/actual). The four-thread version (M3) further halved execution time, with SRA predicting 40% energy reduction from M2 and actual measurements showing 44%. Although estimation errors vary with thread count, the 5% margin suffices for comparisons using SRA energy estimates. Measured and predicted values are strongly correlated, confirming that while more threads increase power dissipation, reduced execution time yields energy savings on the platform.

Another major advantage of NMT is that the gating <cit.> and attention <cit.> techniques prove to be effective in modeling long-distance dependencies and complicated alignment relations in the translation process, which poses a serious challenge for SMT.
new_text: Compared to conventional SMT <cit.>, a key advantage of NMT is that the translation system can be fully developed through data-driven learning without requiring human intervention, in contrast to feature engineering in SMT. Another major advantage of NMT is that the gating <cit.> and attention <cit.> techniques have proven effective in modeling long-distance dependencies and complex alignment relations during the translation process, which present a significant challenge for SMT.

old_text: Coverage problem in NMT: Tu et al. (2016) proposed a coverage mechanism for NMT to alleviate the “over-translation” and “under-translation” problems. They introduced a coverage vector for the attention model, to make the NMT model consider more about untranslated source words in the target word generation. Cohn et al. (2016) enhanced the attention model with structural biases from word based alignment models, including positional bias, Markov conditioning, fertility and agreement over translation directions. Feng et al. (2016) proposed to add implicit distortion and fertility models to attention model. These studies tackle the coverage problem by enhancing the encoder of NMT. As we incorporate SMT model into the decoder part of NMT, our work is complementary to the above studies.
new_text: Tu et al. (2016) introduced a coverage vector to the NMT attention model to address “over-translation” and “under-translation” by tracking untranslated source words during target generation. Cohn et al. (2016) enhanced attention with structural biases from word-based alignment models, such as positional bias, Markov conditioning, fertility, and agreement over translation directions. Feng et al. (2016) integrated implicit distortion and fertility models into the attention mechanism. These approaches address coverage by augmenting the encoder, while our method incorporates an SMT model into the decoder, offering complementary improvements.

old_text: Different from attention-based NMT which predicts the next word based on vector representations, the proposed model makes the prediction also based on recommendations from an SMT model. The SMT model can be separately trained on a bilingual corpus using the conventional phrase-based SMT approach <cit.>. Given decoding information from NMT, the SMT model makes word recommendations[We have not adopted the recently proposed phraseNet which incorporates target phrases into the NMT decoder <cit.>. We leave the investigation to future work.] for the next word prediction with SMT features.
new_text: Unlike attention-based neural machine translation (NMT), which relies solely on vector representations to predict the next word, the proposed model incorporates word recommendations generated by a statistical machine translation (SMT) model. The SMT model is independently trained on a bilingual corpus using a conventional phrase-based SMT framework <cit.>. By utilizing decoding information from the NMT model, the SMT system generates word suggestions that integrate SMT features to enhance the next-word prediction process [We note that the recently proposed phraseNet method, which integrates target phrases into the NMT decoder <cit.>, has not been implemented in this work and remains a topic for future research].

old_text:
We employ an auxiliary classifier to score the SMT recommendations, and use a gating function to linearly combine the two probabilities between the NMT generations and SMT recommendations. The gating function reads the current decoding information, and thus is able to dynamically assign weights to NMT and SMT probabilities at different decoding steps.
Both the SMT classifier and gating function are jointly trained within the NMT architecture in an end-to-end manner.
In addition, to better alleviate the UNK problem in the testing phase, we select a proper SMT recommendation to replace a target UNK word by jointly considering the attention probabilities from the NMT model and the coverage information from the SMT model. Experimental results show that the proposed approach can achieve significant improvements of 2.44 BLEU point over the NMT baseline and 3.21 BLEU point over the Moses (SMT) system on five Chinese-English NIST test sets.
new_text: We employ an auxiliary classifier to score SMT recommendations, providing a probabilistic assessment of their reliability. Simultaneously, a gating function is introduced to linearly integrate the probabilities from NMT-generated outputs and SMT suggestions. This function dynamically adjusts the weighting between the two sources by analyzing real-time decoding context, ensuring adaptability to varying decoding stages. Both components—the SMT classifier and the gating mechanism—are jointly trained within the NMT framework through end-to-end optimization, enabling them to refine their cooperation based on overall system performance. To address the challenge of out-of-vocabulary (UNK) words during testing, the approach leverages a complementary strategy: SMT recommendations are selectively used to replace UNK tokens in NMT outputs. This replacement decision is informed by a dual consideration of NMT attention probabilities (indicating word relevance) and SMT coverage data (marking translation progress), ensuring contextual appropriateness. Evaluations on five Chinese-English NIST test sets demonstrate that this integrated method surpasses the standalone NMT baseline by 2.44 BLEU points and outperforms the Moses SMT system by 3.21 BLEU points, highlighting its effectiveness in harmonizing the strengths of both paradigms.

old_text: We show that our generative representation can be used to synthesize high-quality realistic objects, and our discriminative representation can be used for 3D object recognition, achieving comparable performance with recent supervised methods <cit.>, and outperforming other unsupervised methods by a large margin. The learned generative and discriminative representations also have wide applications. For example, we show that our network can be combined with a variational autoencoder <cit.> to directly reconstruct a 3D object from a 2D input image. Further, we explore the space of object representations and demonstrate that both our generative and discriminative representations carry rich semantic information about 3D objects.
new_text: We demonstrate that our generative representation enables the synthesis of high-quality, realistic 3D objects, while the discriminative representation supports effective 3D object recognition. In recognition tasks, our method achieves performance levels comparable to recent supervised approaches and significantly outperforms other unsupervised methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our learned representations in capturing essential features for both generation and recognition. The utility of these representations extends beyond their primary applications. For instance, by integrating our network with a variational autoencoder, we can directly reconstruct 3D objects from 2D input images, demonstrating the compatibility of our framework with established generative models. Furthermore, our analysis of the representation space reveals that both generative and discriminative features encode rich semantic information about 3D objects. This semantic richness suggests that the representations capture meaningful structural and functional attributes, which could enhance tasks requiring deeper object understanding or manipulation.

section: Related work: Pooling in CNNs for dense prediction on images
old_text:
To incorporate both global and local information,
downsampling pooling has been incorporated in dense prediction networks in several ways.
Firstly, many methods involve upsampling lower resolution feature maps, usually
combined with some higher resolution feature maps.
In <cit.>, an image is processed at three different scales
with three different CNNs, after which the output feature maps are merged.
The Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs) from <cit.> use a VGG classification network
as basis, introducing skip connections to merge hi-res lower layers with upsampled low-res
layers from deeper in the network.
new_text: To integrate global and local information, downsampling pooling has been integrated into dense prediction networks through various approaches. A common strategy involves upsampling lower-resolution feature maps and integrating them with higher-resolution features. In <cit.>, images are processed at three distinct scales using three separate CNNs, followed by the combination of their output feature maps. The Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs) presented in <cit.> build on a VGG classification network, leveraging skip connections to merge high-resolution features from earlier layers with upsampled low-resolution features from deeper network layers.

old_text: Implementation: A total of 3 different DelugeNet models are implemented and evaluated on CIFAR datasets. Similar to <cit.><cit.>, all the 3 DelugeNet models have 3 blocks - the first block works on spatially 32×32 feature maps, followed by 16×16 and 8×8 feature maps for second and third blocks respectively. They vary only in terms of numbers of composite layers and feature channel dimensions for the 3 blocks. To minimize manual tuning of architectural hyperparameters, we design different DelugeNet models based on a simple principle - the second block has 2 times the numbers of composite layers and feature channel dimension (width) of the first block, the third block has 3 times of the first's, and so on:
new_text: To evaluate the performance of the proposed architecture, three distinct DelugeNet models were implemented and tested on the CIFAR datasets. These models follow a shared structural framework, as described in previous studies <cit.><cit.>, each consisting of three sequential blocks that process feature maps at progressively reduced spatial resolutions. Specifically, the first block operates on 32×32 feature maps, the second block processes 16×16 feature maps, and the third block handles 8×8 feature maps. The key distinction among the three models lies in the configuration of composite layers and feature channel dimensions within each block. To reduce the need for manual hyperparameter tuning, the models are designed according to a systematic scaling rule: for every block, the number of composite layers and the feature channel width increase proportionally. For instance, the second block is designed with twice the number of composite layers and twice the channel width of the first block, while the third block triples these values relative to the first. This approach ensures a structured exploration of model capacity while maintaining consistency in architectural progression.

old_text: There is another stream of works focusing on improving the information flows between layers of very deep networks, which is also the focus of our work. Highway Networks <cit.> make use of a Long-Short-Term-Memory (LSTM <cit.>)-inspired gating mechanism to control information flow from linear and nonlinear pathways. Through appropriately learned gating functions, information can flow unimpededly across many layers. He et al. <cit.> propose Residual Networks (ResNets) which compute the residual (additive) functions of the outputs of linear and nonlinear pathways, without complex gating mechanisms. ResNets have shown to tackle well the vanishing gradient and network degradation problems that occur in very deep networks. Later, a pre-activation variant of residual building block <cit.> (ResNet-v2) is proposed to significantly enhance information flow and regularization of ResNet models. Instead of going deeper, Wide-ResNets <cit.> improve upon originally proposed ResNets by having more convolutional filters/channels (width) and less numbers of layers (depth). Motivated by the high model complexity of ResNets in terms of depths and parameter numbers, several “dropping"-based regularization methods <cit.><cit.> have been developed for regularizing large ResNet models. ResNets can be seen as a less flexible special case of DelugeNets, in which the cross-layer connection weights are not learnable and fixed as ones. Densely connected networks (DenseNets) <cit.> which we discuss extensively in Section <ref> belong to the same stream of works.
new_text: Our work aligns with research on enhancing information flow in deep networks. Highway Networks <cit.> employ LSTM-inspired gating mechanisms to regulate linear and nonlinear pathways, enabling seamless multilayer flow via learned gates. ResNets <cit.> compute residual functions of these pathways without complex gates, effectively addressing vanishing gradients and network degradation. ResNet-v2 <cit.> introduces pre-activation blocks to enhance flow and regularization. Wide-ResNets <cit.> improve ResNets by increasing width (filters) while reducing depth. To address ResNet complexity in depth and parameters, 'dropping'-based regularization methods <cit.><cit.> have been developed. ResNets represent a less flexible DelugeNets variant, with fixed cross-layer connection weights set to one. Densely connected networks (DenseNets <cit>), extensively discussed in Section <ref>, fall into this category.

old_text: To facilitate massive and flexible cross-layer information inflows, in this paper, we develop a cross-layer depthwise convolution method. A cross-layer depthwise convolutional layer concatenates the channels of feature map outputs of many layers, and then applies (channel,spatial)-independent filters to the concatenated channels. Equipped with such filters, DelugeNets are able to process the depth/layer dimension independently of the rest (channel and spatial dimensions), as mentioned in Section <ref>. Figure <ref> gives a graphical illustration of cross-layer depthwise convolution operation.

new_text: Mahlmann and Schindelhauer proved that the flip chain is irreducible on Ω_F <cit.>. For all states x ∈ Ω_F, the self-loop probability satisfies P(x, x) ≥ 1/(2r), as the proposed transition is rejected whenever c = a. Consequently, the flip chain is aperiodic, and hence ergodic. By <cit.>, this ergodicity implies that the smallest eigenvalue λ_{N−1} of ℳ_F satisfies (1 + λ_{N−1})^{-1} ≤ r. This bound, in turn, permits application of the canonical path method without modifying the chain to be lazy, as the resulting upper bound on (1 − λ_1)^{-1} will significantly exceed r.

Previous work on CNNs for acoustic modeling <cit.>
eliminated the possibility of strided pooling in time because of the downsampling effect.
Recent work <cit.> shows a significant performance boost
by using pooling in time during cross-entropy training, however sequence training is prohibitively

By adapting the notion of dense prediction, we propose to allow pooling in time while maintaining

with dilation in the time direction but not in the frequency direction,

Recent work <cit.> demonstrated a performance boost using temporal pooling in cross-entropy training; however, sequence training remains costly as utterances require segmentation into `uttLen` independent windows. We propose enabling temporal pooling via asymmetric spatial dilated convolutions with dilation solely in the time dimension—termed time-dilated convolutions—to maintain full-utterance efficiency.

new_text: To engage the general public in reflecting on media bias, we deployed one of the bots from the UnbiasedCrowd project on Twitter. This bot shared tweets featuring image macros created by activists, which were designed to highlight potential visual biases in news coverage of Mexico’s energy reform. Each tweet posed a direct question asking users whether they perceived a bias in how the media was reporting the issue. By structuring the bot’s interactions this way, we aimed to encourage users to critically evaluate media content and articulate their perspectives. If a user responded to the bot or mentioned it in a tweet, the bot automatically followed up with pre-scripted questions about what steps should be taken to address the identified visual bias, fostering further engagement and reflection. These interactions were guided by the methodological framework outlined in <cit.>, which emphasizes structured engagement to elicit actionable insights from public participation. To uphold ethical standards, we implemented rigorous protocols. All users targeted by the bot were informed about the study after completing their interaction and given the opportunity to opt out of the research. Those who chose to opt out had their data excluded from analysis; ultimately, all participants consented to the use of their data for the study.

In the previous work based on paraphrasing <cit.>, semantic parsers are implemented as log-linear models with hand-engineered domain-specific features (including paraphrase features).
Considering the recent success of representation learning for domain adaptation <cit.>, we propose a paraphrase model based on the sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model <cit.>, which can be trained end to end without feature engineering.
We show that it outperforms the previous log-linear models by a large margin in the in-domain setting, and can easily adapt to new domains.
new_text: In prior research on paraphrase modeling <cit.>, semantic parsers were implemented using log-linear models that relied on hand-engineered domain-specific features, such as paraphrase patterns. These approaches required substantial manual effort to design and extract relevant features tailored to specific tasks or domains. However, recent advancements in representation learning techniques that facilitate domain adaptation <cit.> have shifted the paradigm. Leveraging these developments, we propose a paraphrase model based on sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) architectures <cit.>. Unlike the earlier models, this approach eliminates the need for manual feature engineering, enabling end-to-end training by directly learning representations from raw data. Empirically, we demonstrate that the Seq2Seq-based model significantly outperforms the prior log-linear baselines in in-domain settings, achieving improvements by a large margin. Furthermore, its learned representations generalize effectively, allowing straightforward adaptation to new domains without extensive re-engineering.

Notice that dealing with negative results is a very controversial topic and still unsettled in many fields. So, do not expect this writing to touch on all of the aspects. Rather, here, I try to shed light on some less explored matters and put computer vision in a broader perspective with respect to science in general, and its related fields such as Neuroscience and Cognitive Science, in particular. Indeed, further discussion is needed in the vision community to converge to a consensus regarding treatment of negative results.
new_text: Addressing negative results remains a contentious and unresolved issue across numerous disciplines. This work does not aspire to cover every facet; instead, it aims to highlight under-examined areas and position computer vision within a wider scientific framework, particularly in relation to fields like Neuroscience and Cognitive Science. Further dialogue within the computer vision community is essential to establish a consensus on addressing negative results.

old_text: Computer vision has its own unique characteristics making it distinct from other fields thereby demanding a specific treatment of negative results. Firstly, vision is an extremely hard problem which has baffled many smart people throughout its history. The complexity of the problem makes it difficult to run controlled experiments and come up with a universal theory of vision. Secondly, often a large number of variables are involved in building vision algorithms and analyzing large scale data. Further, fair comparison of several competing models using multiple scores exacerbates the problem. To address these, it would be very helpful to borrow from other fields (e.g., natural sciences) where experimental design and statistical testing are integral parts of the scientific research.
new_text: Computer vision presents distinct challenges that necessitate specialized consideration of negative outcomes. Vision remains an exceptionally complex challenge, having puzzled researchers across its history, a complexity that complicates the execution of controlled experiments and the formulation of a universal theoretical framework. Additionally, designing vision algorithms involves numerous variables, while analyzing large-scale datasets introduces further layers of difficulty. Complicating matters further, conducting equitable comparisons among competing models using multiple evaluation metrics amplifies these challenges. To mitigate these issues, leveraging methodologies from disciplines such as natural sciences—where rigorous experimental design and statistical validation are foundational to research—could provide valuable insights.

old_text: A related problem here is the issue of replicability. Replicability of findings is believed to be at the heart of empirical sciences <cit.>. As in other fields, computer vision researchers tend not to replicate other people's works for two major reasons. Either it is possible to replicate someone else's work or it is not. In the former case, a reviewer may find your results boring or predictable. In the latter case, you may be accused of not following the right procedure. So, in both case there is a risk factor involved. To mitigate the risks, the community needs to advocate for well-documented solid negative results and educate the reviewers.
new_text: Replicability remains a critical challenge in scientific research, particularly within computer vision. The ability to reproduce findings is a foundational principle in empirical disciplines <cit.>. Researchers in this field often avoid replicating others’ work due to two primary concerns. When replication is feasible, reviewers may perceive the outcomes as unoriginal or predictable; conversely, if replication fails, researchers risk being criticized for methodological flaws. Both scenarios involve inherent risks that deter replication efforts. Addressing this requires a shift in the academic culture: promoting the publication of rigorously documented, credible negative results and fostering reviewer education to better support replication studies.

old_text: Following the flowchart in Figure <ref>, our approach consists of two parts as evidence extraction[In our model, we use “evidence extraction” to represent the pure “answer extraction” in previous work.] and answer generation. The evidence extraction part aims to extract evidence snippets related to the question and passage. We use the gated attention recurrent neural network to match the question and passage, and then use pointer networks to predict the boundary of evidence snippets. new_text:
Our approach, outlined in the step-by-step flowchart of Figure <ref>, is structured into two core components: evidence extraction and answer generation. To clarify terminology, we emphasize that “evidence extraction” in our framework explicitly corresponds to what prior work described as “answer extraction.” This first phase identifies and isolates relevant segments (evidence snippets) from the passage that are pertinent to the given question. To achieve this, we employ a gated attention recurrent neural network to align the question and passage, capturing contextual dependencies. This is followed by pointer networks, which predict the start and end positions of the evidence snippets within the passage.  

The second phase—answer generation—builds on the extracted evidence to construct the final response. Here, we utilize a sequence-to-sequence model, where the evidence snippets serve as input. To enhance performance, we annotate the boundaries of the extracted evidence as an additional feature during the encoding stage. Furthermore, an attention-equipped decoder is applied to focus on the most salient parts of the evidence when generating the answer, ensuring coherence and relevance in the final output.

old_text: Recent conditional image generation models, such as Attribute2image <cit.>, given an input image and a desired attribute vector they can generate images that have those attributes, e.g., “old", “male", “brown hair" etc. Such models are trained with strong supervision, where each training image is annotated with a set of attributes. Attribute "progression" ( e.gchanging male to female) is achieved by varying the value of the target attribute in the input vector. In the experimental section, we compare our model against Attribute2Image and show our result better preserves the fidelity of the transformation and has higher level of detail, at the negligible cost of training a different super-resolution or inpainting model for each desired transformation. Further, our transformations can reflect fine-grained visual attributes described by a set of exemplar images (as discriminator memories), e.g., we can transform a face to be more like Tom Cruise or have Michael Jackson nose. This is not possible with previous supervised models whose transformations are described by coarse attribute categories, e.g., “old".
new_text: Recent conditional image generation models, including Attribute2image <cit.>, produce images by taking an input image and a desired attribute vector (e.g., “old”, “male”, “brown hair”) to create outputs with those characteristics. These systems require strong supervision, where each training image is labeled with specific attributes. Gradual attribute transitions, such as shifting from “male” to “female”, are enabled by adjusting the target attribute’s value in the input vector. In our experiments, we compare our approach to Attribute2Image, demonstrating improved preservation of transformation fidelity and enhanced detail, albeit with the requirement of training distinct super-resolution or inpainting models for each transformation, a minimal overhead. Additionally, our method supports fine-grained visual adjustments guided by exemplar images (serving as discriminator memories), such as morphing a face to resemble Tom Cruise or incorporating Michael Jackson’s nose. Prior supervised models are limited to coarse attribute categories like “old”, making such precise, example-based transformations impossible.

old_text: Formally proving the correctness of a program with respect to a given specification, can be largely automated when the appropriate program invariants are available. Yet, the problem of learning the adequate invariants in the first place, remains quite challenging. Traditional white-box or static inference approaches that reason over the program structure to deduce sufficient invariants, are often inapplicable to real-life cases simply because the program logic is far too complex to be analyzable. However, it is often the case that many complex real-life programs have relatively simple invariants that certify their correctness relative to properties of practical interest. In such cases, black-box or data-driven inference techniques seem to perform well. These techniques learn a candidate invariant by examining program behavior (as opposed to structure), and then refine it till it is sufficiently strong.
new_text: Formally verifying a program's compliance with a specification can be highly automated when suitable invariants are present. However, identifying the correct invariants remains a significant challenge. Traditional white-box or static inference methods, which deduce invariants through program structure analysis, often struggle with real-world applications due to their complexity. Despite this, many real-world programs exhibit simple invariants that confirm their correctness regarding important properties. In these scenarios, black-box or data-driven inference approaches prove effective. These techniques derive potential invariants by observing program execution patterns and iteratively refine them to achieve the necessary strength.

One approach is known as model-based method, the idea of which is to propose a parametric probabilistic model characterize the clustering structure of a social network. Popular probabilistic models include the stochastic block model in <cit.>, a latent position cluster model in <cit.>, and a mixed membership block model in <cit.>, etc. Another approach is called clique-based method, of which the core is to specify an objective function based on some metric that can be used to quantitatively evaluate the quality of social network clustering; the objective is to design an efficient algorithm to optimize the objective function. old_text: We incorporate information about joint angle limits and bone length constraints, using three regularization terms in the loss function. In the first term we penalize illegal extension of the knee and elbow joints. Human elbows and knees are constrained to move within a limited angle of flexion while extensions are physically not possible. Penalizing such poses pushes the ConvNet away from the space of implausible poses. In the second regularization term, we penalize asymmetric lengths of left/right bone pairs. We also use the geometric regularization proposed in <cit.>. These three terms together provide highly effective depth supervision in the absence of 3D-labeled data, and guide the model towards better local minima. We validate the effectiveness of our approach by quantitative as well as qualitative evaluations (Section <ref>). Using our structure-aware loss function alone, we improve the Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE) over the state-of-the-art on Human 3.6M dataset by 6%, and MPI-INF-3DHP test set by 7.7%.
new_text: We incorporate information on joint angle limits and bone length constraints by using three regularization terms in the loss function. In the first term, we penalize unphysical extensions of the knee and elbow joints. Human elbows and knees are constrained to flex within a limited range, while full extension is physically impossible. Penalizing such poses constrains the ConvNet to avoid the space of implausible configurations. In the second regularization term, we penalize asymmetric bone lengths of left and right limb pairs. We also use the geometric regularization proposed in <cit.>. Together, these three terms provide highly effective depth supervision without the need for 3D-labeled data and guide the model toward more optimal local minima. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through both quantitative and qualitative evaluations (Section <ref>). Using our structure-aware loss function alone, we improve the Mean Per-Joint Position Error (MPJPE) over the state-of-the-art on the Human3.6M dataset by 6%, and on the MPI-INF-3DHP test set by 7.7%.

In this paper, we describe how to efficiently implement
an acoustic room simulator to generate large-scale
simulated data for training deep neural networks.
We implement an efficient OverLap
Addition (OLA) based filtering using the open-source `FFTW3`
library. We investigate into the effects of the Room
Impulse Response (RIR) lengths. We conclude that we can cut
the tail portions of RIRs whose power is less than 20 dB
below the maximum power without sacrificing speech recognition accuracy.
However, if we cut off RIR more than that, we observe it adversely
affects the performance for reverberant cases.
Using the approaches mentioned here, we could reduce the
room simulator portion in the CPU usage down to 9.69 %
in CPU/GPU training architecture. Profiling result shows that
we obtain 22.4 times speed-up on a local desktop machine and 37.3 times
speed up on `Google Borg` cluster.
new_text: We describe an efficient acoustic room simulator for generating large-scale simulated data to train deep neural networks. Using the open-source `FFTW3` library, we implement efficient OverLap Addition (OLA)-based filtering. We investigate Room Impulse Response (RIR) length effects and find that cutting RIR tails with power <20 dB below the maximum power does not impact speech recognition accuracy, but further cuts harm reverberant performance. The approaches reduce room simulator CPU usage to 9.69% in CPU/GPU training architecture. Profiling results show 22.4× speed-up on a desktop and 37.3× on a `Google Borg` cluster.

old_text: Duration distributions For ordinary HMMs, the time spent in each state follows a geometric distribution. However, this parameterization does not describe many real-world cycles. For example, a “weekend state” in human activity data (e.g., longer sleep during the weekend) might reliably last two days and would be poorly described by a geometric distribution. Similarly, the length of the luteal phase in the human menstrual cycle is better described by a normal distribution <cit.>. In particular, the monotonicity of the geometric probability mass function makes it a poor approximation to many real-world distributions. Instead, we use Poisson distributions for the duration distributions 𝒟_j, so each duration distribution for the j-th latent state is parameterized by a single rate parameter λ_j. We use Poisson distributions for several reasons: they are frequently used in HSMMs; they are fast to fit and easy to interpret; and we will show empirically that they provide a better fit to real-world cycles than do geometric distributions. If a distribution with more flexibility were desired, a negative binomial, hypergeometric, or non-parametric distribution could be used.
new_text: In ordinary HMMs, duration distributions follow a geometric distribution, which is unsuitable for many real-world cycles. For instance, a weekend state in human activity data might reliably last two days, while luteal phases in the human menstrual cycle are better described by a normal distribution <cit.>. The geometric distribution’s monotonic probability mass function limits its applicability. To address this, we use Poisson distributions for durations 𝒟_j, parameterized by rate λ_j. We employ Poisson distributions for three reasons: their common use in HSMMs; computational efficiency and interpretability; and empirical evidence showing superior fits to real-world cycles compared to geometric distributions. Alternatives like negative binomial or non-parametric models could offer greater flexibility if needed.

Menstrual cycles dataset The human menstrual cycle is fundamental to women's health; features of the cycle have been linked to cancer <cit.>, depression <cit.>, and sports injuries <cit.>, and the cycle has been proposed as a vital sign <cit.>.
We obtained data from one of the most popular menstrual cycle tracking apps. Upon logging into the app, users can record binary features including period/cycle start (e.g., light, moderate, or heavy bleeding), mood (e.g., happy, sad, or sensitive), pain (e.g., cramps or headache) or sexual activity (e.g., protected or unprotected sex). We define the start of each menstrual cycle as the start of period bleeding. We confirmed that statistics of the dataset were consistent with existing literature on the menstrual cycle: the average cycle duration was 28 days, consistent with previous investigations, and features that peaked before the cycle start were consistent with previous investigations of premenstrual syndrome <cit.>.

old_text: A common and relatively simple class of queries are statistical queries <cit.>. A statistical query is specified by a function ψ:→ [0,1] and corresponds to analyst wishing to compute the true mean X∼𝒫ψ(X) of ψ on the data distribution 𝒫. (This is usually done by using the empirical mean 1/n∑_i=1^n ψ(S_i) on a dataset S consisting of n i.i.d. draws from the distribution 𝒫.) For example, such queries can be used to to estimate the true loss (or error) of a predictor, the gradient of the loss function, or the moments of the data distribution. Standard concentration results imply that, given n independent samples from 𝒫, k fixed (i.e. not adaptively-chosen) statistical queries can be answered with an additive error of at most O ( √(log(k)/n)) with high probability by simply using the empirical mean of each query. At the same time it is not hard to show that, for a variety of simple adaptive sequences of queries, using the empirical mean to estimate the expectation leads to an error of Ω(√(k/n)) <cit.>. Equivalently, in the adaptive setting, the number of samples required to ensure fixed error scales linearly (rather than logarithmically in the non-adaptive setting) with the number of queries and, in particular, in the worst case, using empirical estimates gives the same guarantees as using fresh samples for every query (by splitting the dataset into k parts).
new_text: Statistical queries form a common class of data analysis tasks <cit.>. Each query is defined by a function ψ:→ [0,1] and seeks to compute the true mean E_{X∼𝒫}[ψ(X)] over distribution 𝒫, typically estimated using the empirical mean 1/n ∑_{i=1}^n ψ(S_i) for n i.i.d. samples S from 𝒫. Such queries can estimate predictor loss/error, gradients, or distribution moments. Standard concentration bounds guarantee that k fixed (non-adaptive) queries yield an additive error of at most O(√(log k/n)) with high probability via empirical means. However, for simple adaptive query sequences, the empirical mean estimation leads to Ω(√(k/n)) error <cit.>. This implies that in adaptive settings, sample requirements scale linearly with query count (rather than logarithmically in non-adaptive settings), with worst-case guarantees equivalent to using fresh samples per query via dataset partitioning.

We argue that RNN encoder adds extra complication to the encoder but is actually not necessary, and the approach can be made much more general by omitting it.Edits to this sentence OK? Actually check whole paragraph. RNNs are necessary only when the inputs convey sequential information; e.g., in text translation the combination of words and their relative position must be captured in order for the translation to be accurate. But the question here is, why do we need to have them in the encoder for combinatorial optimization problems when there is no meaningful order in the input set? As an example, in the TSP, the inputs are the set of unordered city locations, and their order is not meaningful; any random permutation contains the same information as the original inputs. Therefore, in our model, we simply leave out the encoder RNN and directly use the embedded inputs instead of the RNN hidden states. By this modification, many of the computational complications disappear, without decreasing the model's efficiency.
new_text: We argue that the RNN encoder introduces unnecessary complexity to the architecture and is not essential, as the approach can be generalized more effectively by omitting it. RNNs are necessary only when the inputs inherently involve sequential information; for instance, in text translation, the sequence of words and their relative positions must be preserved for accurate results. However, in combinatorial optimization problems—where the input set lacks a meaningful order—RNNs become superfluous. Consider the TSP, where the input consists of an unordered set of city locations; the order of these locations is irrelevant, as any permutation conveys the same information as the original input. In our model, we therefore remove the encoder RNN and directly employ embedded inputs in place of RNN-derived hidden states. This modification eliminates many computational complexities while maintaining the model’s efficiency.

Finally, in Figure <ref> we consider three heuristic metrics for measuring the exploratory ability of the meta-learners. First, we consider the fraction of tile types visited by the agent at test time. Our intuition is that good exploratory agents will visit and identify many different tile types as this should aid in optimally solving the game. Second, we consider the number of times an agent visits a death tile at test time. Agents that are efficient at exploring should visit this tile type exactly once and then avoid it. We often find that more naive agents will run into these tiles repeatedly, causing their death many times over and a sense of pity in any onlookers. Finally, we look at how many goals the agent reaches. We see that RL^2 tends to visit fewer goals and instead tend to stick with a strategy of finding one goal and exploiting it. Overall, we see that the exploratory algorithms achieve better performance under these metrics.
new_text: In Figure <ref>, we evaluate three heuristic metrics to assess the exploratory capabilities of the meta-learners. First, we analyze the proportion of unique tile types explored by the agent during testing, hypothesizing that effective exploration would lead to increased identification of diverse tile types, thereby supporting optimal game-solving strategies. Second, we measure how frequently agents encounter death tiles at test time. An efficient explorer should theoretically interact with such tiles only once and subsequently avoid them, whereas less sophisticated agents often repeatedly collide with them, resulting in repeated failures. Finally, we quantify the number of goals reached, noting that RL² agents tend to prioritize a single goal and exploit it rather than seeking multiple objectives. Across these metrics, exploratory algorithms demonstrate superior performance compared to alternative approaches.

new_text: Intrinsic motivation can be implemented by modeling the expected learning progress ζ(s,a) of a state-action pair <cit.>. The perception (Sec. <ref>) and the action (Sec. <ref>) objectives previously described are both necessary for vision-based quadrotor navigation.

Indeed, for a quadrotor to track a reference trajectory, it needs to rotate to align its thrust with the direction of the desired acceleration.

A model-based optimization framework able to consider both perception and action objectives and couple them through the system dynamics is therefore necessary.

new_text: In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive large-scale study comparing the effectiveness of various acquisition functions across three distinct tasks: Sentiment Classification (SC), Named Entity Recognition (NER), and Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). To ensure robust and generalizable findings, our experiments span multiple datasets, models, and acquisition functions for each task, enabling a nuanced evaluation of performance under diverse conditions. A key methodological feature of our approach is the use of warm-start data to set hyperparameters. This practice avoids overfitting to validation data during training and ensures a fairer comparison by grounding all experiments on a consistent baseline. Rather than advocating for a specific acquisition function or model architecture, our goal is to investigate whether any method consistently demonstrates reliable performance across tasks when applied without extensive task-specific tuning. This inquiry seeks to address a practical challenge in active learning: can a single strategy serve as a dependable default for new problems?

imposes a prior over the weights,

Person Re-identification (ReID).
Person reID <cit.> is a challenging task due to various human poses, domain differences, occlusions, etc.
Two main types of methods were adopted in previous works, i.e. learning discriminative person representations <cit.> and metric learning <cit.>.
PAN <cit.> aligns pedestrians and learn person features simultaneously without any extra annotation.
Zhao et al. <cit.> proposed SpindleNet for learning person features of different body regions with additional human pose information.
Most recent methods <cit.> designed more complicated frameworks to learn more robust representations with increasing computational cost or requiring extra information during inference.
new_text: Person Re-identification (ReID) remains a complex task due to factors such as diverse human postures, cross-domain variations, and partial occlusions. Prior studies have focused on two primary approaches: learning discriminative person representations <cit.> and refining similarity metrics through metric learning <cit.>. Methods like PAN <cit.> integrate pedestrian alignment and feature extraction into a unified framework without relying on supplementary annotations. In contrast, Zhao et al. introduced SpindleNet <cit.>, which leverages human pose data to model region-specific person features. However, recent approaches <cit.> have shifted toward increasingly sophisticated architectures to enhance representation robustness, often at the cost of higher computational demands or reliance on external data during inference.
