old_text: In conformity with previous studies, speech input modality is overall less distracting to drivers than manual input modality <cit.>. Moreover, according to the MRT the combination of audio output and speech input is expected to be the least detrimental to driving performance, because auditory perception and verbal response are barely needed by the driving task. However, the optimum combination of input and output modality varies in terms of different dependent variables. For lateral control, audio-speech modality does produce the least steering error. With regard to longitudinal control, audio-speech modality results in highest approaching speed in hazard event; while in lane changing task, the highest average approaching speed occurs under visual-speech modality. This difference may be caused by the distinction between the driving contexts of hazard events and lane changing tasks <cit.>. With respect to the hazard detection, the drivers fastest react to the hazard events under speech-visual modality, and maintain the longest minimum headway time under speech-combined modality, which could be regarded as speech-visual modality because their minor difference (speech-combined: M=1.175, SD= 0.119; speech-visual: M=1.171, SD= 0.108) and that visual component dominates the combined modality as stated above. The reason might associate with the drivers' gaze concentration. Unlike the lane changing task and car following task, the hazard events occur during normal driving, which does not require drivers' visual attention to any specific spot of the driving scene. So drivers tend to concentrate their gaze in the center of the driving scene when order of audio-speech modality introduces cognitive distraction to them, and thus their ability to detect targets across the entire driving scene is diminished <cit.>. When handling order of visual-speech modality, drivers incline to consciously saccade the whole driving scene after short off-road glance (to get the order information) in order to comprehend the new driving contexts, and thus observe the pulling-out car sooner.
new_text: Speech input modality is less distracting to drivers than manual input <cit.>. According to the MRT, audio output paired with speech input minimizes driving performance decline, as auditory perception and verbal response are seldom required for driving tasks. Optimal modality combinations vary by dependent variable: audio-speech modality yields lowest steering error for lateral control; highest approaching speed in hazard events for longitudinal control; and highest average approaching speed in lane changing tasks under visual-speech modality. These differences likely stem from contextual distinctions between hazard events and lane changes <cit.>. For hazard detection, drivers react fastest to hazards under speech-visual modality and maintain the longest minimum headway under speech-combined modality (speech-combined: M=1.175, SD=0.119; speech-visual: M=1.171, SD=0.108), reflecting the visual dominance in combined modalities. This may relate to gaze concentration: hazard events during normal driving do not require directed visual attention, so cognitive distraction from audio-speech modality reduces drivers’ peripheral awareness. Conversely, visual-speech modality prompts brief off-road glances to process order information, followed by scene-wide saccades to comprehend new contexts, enabling earlier detection of hazards <cit.>.

Motivated by the development of artificial intelligence, there has been a good amount of progress in image recognition over the past 10 years, including the proposal of many new models and the creation of benchmark datasets.
In some papers, however, there is a tendency to compare models only on one or two datasets, either because of time restraints or because the model is tailored to a specific task. Accordingly, it is hard to understand how well a certain model generalizes across image recognition field.
In this paper, our main contributions are, therefore, comparing four mainstream image recognition models on MNIST dataset with different division. Among of them, three are CNN, ResNet and DenseNet respectively. These three models are already proved to have good performance in image recognition, and we summarize the characteristics of these models in Section 2. In addition, we find that the standard CNN model still exists some drawbacks. Accordingly we use CNN as a baseline model, and improve it through applying CapsNet to optimize on this basis. It is the fourth model and is described in detail in Section 3. We use the MNIST dataset for the test because the recognition of handwritten digits is a topic of practical importance. This object has continued to produce much research effort in recent years for several reasons. First, standard benchmark datasets like MNIST exist that make it easy for us to obtain result. Second, many publications and techniques are available that can be cited and built on, respectively. In order to make the model more generalizable in the field of image recognition, we randomly divided the MNIST dataset into 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% to test.
Ultimately, we contribute to a better understanding of the performance of different model architectures on MNIST dataset. Consequently, we detect that CapsNet is the best overall model, which outperforms the other models on all tasks and consistently beats the baseline. The results of experiment are presented in Section 4, and conclusion follows in Section 5.

The network architecture for the generator and discriminator follows the ResBlocks architecture introduced by <cit.>. Following SAGAN <cit.>, we use spectral normalization for all layers in the discriminator. We add a self-attention layer to the intermediate layers with spatial dimensions 16 × 16 for the discriminator and the generator. The image encoders E_G and E_D have separate parameters, as they have to be optimized for adversarial objectives, the generator's and the discriminator's respectively. For the training dynamics, the generator and discriminator parameters are updated every time step, while the encoders' parameters are updated every sequence. The text encoder and the GRU are trained with respect to the discriminator objective only. For training, we use teacher forcing with the ground truth images x_t-1 instead of the generated image x_t-1, but we use x_t-1 during test time. Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix <ref>.
new_text: The generator and discriminator network architectures employ the ResBlocks framework first presented by <cit.>. Adhering to the SAGAN methodology <cit.>, spectral normalization is applied to every layer within the discriminator. Both the generator and discriminator incorporate self-attention modules at intermediate 16 × 16 spatial resolutions. The image encoders E_G and E_D maintain distinct parameter sets due to their distinct adversarial optimization targets—generator-centric and discriminator-centric objectives, respectively. During training, the generator and discriminator parameters are updated iteratively per time step, whereas encoder parameters undergo updates only at sequence intervals. old_text: As discussed, current public datasets provide limited information regarding the actors' physical characteristics such as age, height, weight etc. which is insufficient in order to accurately assess the impact of these characteristics on fall detection algorithms. Sometimes, the authors of these studies state the gender of the participants without specifying however, further information. Also, the number of fall events or of the participating actors is limited when compared to other action recognition datasets, due to the risks involved. In addition, these public datasets do not include data of the specific group for which they are usually intended i.e. the older people and people with disabilities and they have limited variability in terms of physical characteristics. Also, most of these datasets lack visual occlusions hence, there are no means to develop occlusion robust algorithms or assess their effectiveness. These issues may have serious implications in the deployment of fall detection systems in the wild.
new_text: As discussed, current public datasets offer insufficient details about participants' physical attributes—such as age, height, and weight—which are critical factors in evaluating how these traits influence fall detection algorithms. Without this data, researchers cannot adequately analyze whether age-related mobility changes or body mass distribution affect fall patterns or algorithm accuracy. Moreover, while some studies report participants' gender, they rarely include additional relevant demographic or health-related information, such as pre-existing conditions or mobility impairments, further limiting the scope of analysis. Additionally, the number of fall events and total participants in these datasets is typically low compared to datasets for general action recognition tasks, due to ethical and practical concerns surrounding fall simulation or real-world data collection. This reduced sample size weakens the statistical power of studies, making it difficult to generalize findings. Compounding these issues, many public datasets exclude the very populations most in need of fall detection systems, such as older adults and individuals with disabilities, and exhibit limited diversity in physical characteristics. This lack of representativeness hinders the development of inclusive algorithms that account for varied movement patterns and vulnerabilities. Furthermore, these datasets often omit scenarios involving visual occlusions (e.g., objects or people blocking the subject), which are common in real-world settings. The absence of such data prevents the development and testing of algorithms robust to partial visibility, a critical requirement for reliable deployment in uncontrolled environments. Collectively, these limitations pose significant challenges for creating fall detection systems that perform effectively in practical applications, where variability in user demographics, environmental conditions, and occlusion dynamics are unavoidable.

old_text: No manual labels Like existing methods, our framework relies on a manually labeled training dataset. When there are no such training dataset, our framework may also be applicable. Specifically, Wang et al. <cit.> recently proposed SybilBlind, which generalizes LBP-based collective classification methods to the scenarios where no training dataset is available. Their key idea is to randomly sample some nodes from the graph and treat them as labeled nodes (some of them would be labeled incorrectly, i.e., the training data has noise). Then, they apply a LBP-based method with the sampled training data. Since LBP-based methods are robust to some noise in training data, they repeat the sampling process multiple times and design some method to select the sampling trials that have small label noise. We believe such idea can also be applied to our framework when no manual labels are available, because our framework is also robust to some noise in training data.
new_text: Like existing methods, our framework relies on a manually labeled training dataset. However, when no such training dataset is available, our framework may still be applicable. Specifically, Wang et al. <cit.> recently proposed SybilBlind, an approach that generalizes LBP-based collective classification to scenarios without training data. Their method involves randomly sampling nodes from the graph and treating them as labeled nodes, although some are incorrectly labeled, introducing noise into the training data. They then apply an LBP-based method using this sampled data. Since LBP-based methods are resilient to certain levels of noise, they repeat the sampling process multiple times and develop a technique to select trials with minimal label noise. We believe this approach could also be applied to our framework in cases where no manual labels are available, as our framework shares similar robustness to noisy training data.

old_text: Typically, a salient object detection (SOD) model faces opposite requirements in processing object interiors and boundaries. The features of interiors should be invariant to strong appearance change so as to pop-out the salient object as a whole, while the features of boundaries should be selective to slight appearance change to distinguish salient objects and background. To address this selectivity-invariance dilemma, we propose a novel boundary-aware network with successive dilation for image-based SOD. In this network, the feature selectivity at boundaries is enhanced by incorporating a boundary localization stream, while the feature invariance at interiors is guaranteed with a complex interior perception stream. Moreover, a transition compensation stream is adopted to amend the probable failures in transitional regions between interiors and boundaries. In particular, an integrated successive dilation module is proposed to enhance the feature invariance at interiors and transitional regions. Extensive experiments on four datasets show that the proposed approach outperforms 11 state-of-the-art methods.
new_text: Salient object detection (SOD) typically requires resolving conflicting demands between object interiors and boundaries. For interiors, features must remain invariant to significant appearance variations to ensure the entire salient object is detected, while boundaries demand sensitivity to minor appearance shifts to differentiate objects from the background. To resolve this invariance-selectivity trade-off, we introduce a boundary-aware network with successive dilation for image-based SOD. This architecture enhances boundary feature selectivity through a dedicated boundary localization stream, while a complex interior perception stream ensures invariance within object interiors. A transition compensation stream is further incorporated to correct errors in transitional areas between interiors and boundaries. Additionally, an integrated successive dilation module is designed to reinforce invariance in interiors and transitional regions. Comprehensive experiments across four datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses 11 existing state-of-the-art approaches.

old_text: In addition, many models <cit.> comprehend saliency detection task from other perspectives by relating other tasks or cures with SOD. Li et al. <cit.> considered contours as useful priors and proposed to facilitate feature learning in SOD by transferring knowledge from an existing contour detection model. Chen et al. <cit.> proposed reverse attention mechanism which is inspired from human perception process by using top information to guide bottom-up feed-forward process in a top-down manner. Chen et al. <cit.> incorporated human fixation with semantic information to simulate the human annotation process for salient objects. Chen and Li <cit.> proposed a complementarity-aware network to fuse both cross-model and cross-level features to solve saliency detection task with depth information.
new_text: Alternatively, many models <cit.> approach the saliency detection task (SOD) by integrating related tasks or concepts to enhance performance. Li et al. <cit.> developed a method leveraging contour detection as a prior to enhance feature learning in SOD via knowledge transfer from pre-trained contour models. Chen et al. <cit.> introduced a reverse attention mechanism inspired by human perception, using higher-level information to guide a top-down refinement of the bottom-up feed-forward process. In another approach, Chen et al. <cit.> simulated the human annotation process by combining human fixation data with semantic information to identify salient objects. Furthermore, Chen and Li <cit.> designed a complementarity-aware network to integrate cross-model and cross-level features for SOD, incorporating depth information to improve robustness.

new_text: Leveraging shared features, we implement three distinct streams for boundary localization, interior perception, and transition compensation. The boundary stream is based on the subnetwork ϕ_B(π_B), inspired by the work of <cit.>, which aggregates multi-level common features and fuses them through upsampling and concatenation to produce boundary predictions. old_text: LambdaMART <cit.> is built on MART <cit.>. MART builds a regression tree to model the functional gradient of the cost function of interest which leads to the LambdaRank <cit.> functional gradients. Since we are interested in optimizing NDCG and NDCG is either flat or discontinuous everywhere, LambdaRank uses an approximation to the gradient of the cost, called λ-gradients. The λ-gradient consists of the product of two factors: (1) the RankNet cost <cit.> (a pairwise cross-entropy loss, applied to the logistic of the difference of the model scores), and (2) the NDCG gained by swapping the pair, Δ NDCG. During ranker training, the model uses the available features of the document to optimize the metric and produce a predicted score for each document. For more details, we refer to the corresponding literatures <cit.>.
new_text: LambdaMART <cit.> extends MART <cit.>, a framework that constructs regression trees to model the functional gradient of the cost function of interest, ultimately forming the functional gradients used in LambdaRank <cit.>. To optimize NDCG, which exhibits inherent flatness and discontinuities across its domain, LambdaRank employs an approximation to the cost gradient known as λ-gradients. These λ-gradients are defined as the product of two components: (1) the RankNet cost <cit.>, a pairwise cross-entropy loss computed using the logistic of the difference between model scores for document pairs, and (2) the net gain in NDCG resulting from swapping a specific pair, denoted Δ NDCG. During training, the ranker leverages available document features to iteratively refine the predicted scores that maximize this metric. For a detailed exposition, refer to the relevant literature <cit.>.

We proposed a few techniques to obtain watermark signals from online images and demonstrated the effectiveness of utilizing them in the Bing image search. The high watermark classification accuracy using deep CNN networks implies the potential of designing specific watermark DNN models which could work well on universal watermark classification tasks. We also propose domain based analysis to obtain a complementary watermark signal. Additional watermark signals may be obtained by analyzing domain or text information, such as title and body text, about the online image. This sheds light on the solution to provide better image search quality to the user by effectively demoting watermarked images.
new_text: We introduced several techniques to extract watermark signals from online images and demonstrated their effectiveness in enhancing Bing Image Search. The high watermark classification accuracy achieved using deep CNN networks suggests the potential for developing specialized watermark DNN models that can perform well on universal watermark classification tasks. Additionally, we introduced domain-based analysis to obtain complementary watermark signals. Further watermark signals can be extracted by analyzing domain or text information, such as title and body text, associated with the online image. These approaches highlight a pathway for improving image search quality by effectively demoting watermarked images.

Deep learning follows the same learning procedure as in Algorithm <ref>, but the objective function is non-convex. As a result, the sensitivity analysis methods of Chaudhuri et al. <cit.> do not hold for deep learning as they require strong convexity assumption. Hence, their output and objective perturbation methods are not applicable. An alternative approach is to replace the non-convex function with a convex polynomial function <cit.>, and then use the standard objective perturbation. Application of gradient perturbation requires a bound on the gradient norm. Since the gradient norm can be unbounded in deep learning, gradient perturbation can be used after manually clipping the gradients at each iteration. As noted by Abadi et al. <cit.>, norm clipping provides a sensitivity bound on the gradients which is required for generating noise in gradient perturbation.
new_text: Deep learning employs the same learning procedure as in Algorithm <ref>, but its non-convex objective function invalidates methods requiring strong convexity. Specifically, the sensitivity analysis techniques proposed by Chaudhuri et al. <cit.>—including output and objective perturbation—are inapplicable due to this non-convexity. One approach to address this challenge involves approximating the non-convex function with a convex polynomial function <cit.>, enabling the use of standard objective perturbation. Gradient perturbation, which depends on a bounded gradient norm, faces additional complications in deep learning where gradients can be unbounded. To resolve this, manual gradient clipping must be applied iteratively before gradient perturbation. As Abadi et al. <cit.> emphasize, gradient norm clipping establishes a sensitivity bound essential for noise injection during gradient perturbation.

Complex learning tasks requiring large privacy budget
All of the above works are limited to convex learning problems with binary classification tasks. Adopting their approaches to more complex learning tasks requires higher privacy budgets (see Table <ref>). For instance, the online version of ERM as considered by Jain et al. <cit.> requires ϵ as high as 10 to achieve acceptable utility. Which means that theoretically the model's privacy loss can be as large as e^10. This can allow an adversary to infer the presence or absence of a record from the training set with high confidence.
Further, adopting these binary classification methods for multi-class classification tasks requires even higher ϵ values. As noted by Wu et al. <cit.>, it would require training a separate binary classifier for each class.
Finally, high privacy budgets are required for non-convex learning algorithms, such as deep learning <cit.>. Since the output and objective perturbation methods of Chaudhuri et al. <cit.> are not applicable to non-convex settings, implementations of differentially-private deep learning rely on gradient perturbation in their iterative learning procedure. These methods do not scale to large numbers of training iterations due to the composition theorem of differential privacy which implies that the privacy budget accumulates across iterations. The only exceptions are the works of Phan et al. <cit.> that replace the non-linear functions in deep learning with polynomial approximations and then apply objective perturbation. With this transformation, they achieve high model utility for ϵ = 1, as shown in Table <ref>. However, we note that this polynomial approximation is a non-standard approach to deep learning which can limit the model's learning capacity, and thereby affecting the model accuracy for complex tasks.
new_text:
Complex learning tasks requiring large privacy budgets  
All cited works are limited to convex binary classification problems. Extending these approaches to complex tasks demands higher privacy budgets (Table <ref>). Jain et al. <cit.> demonstrate that their online ERM variant requires ϵ ≥ 10 for acceptable utility, translating to a privacy loss of up to e¹⁰, enabling adversaries to infer training set membership with high confidence. Multi-class adaptations further escalate ϵ requirements, as Wu et al. <cit.> show, necessitating a separate binary classifier per class. For non-convex settings like deep learning <cit.>, output and objective perturbation methods by Chaudhuri et al. <cit.> become inapplicable, forcing reliance on gradient perturbation. However, differential privacy's composition theorem restricts such methods to limited iterations due to cumulative privacy budget depletion. Phan et al. <cit.> bypass this by polynomially approximating deep learning’s non-linearities, enabling objective perturbation at ϵ = 1 (Table <ref>). This non-standard approximation, however, constrains model capacity and degrades performance on complex tasks.

The attack framework of Yeom et al. <cit.> is simpler than Shokri et al.'s design. It assumes a white-box attacker with access to the target model's expected training loss on the private data set, in addition to having access to the target model. For membership inference, the attacker simply observes the target model's loss on the input record. The attacker classifies the record as a member of private data set if the loss is smaller than the target model's expected training loss, otherwise the record is classified as a non-member. The same principle is used for attribute inference. Given an input record, the attacker brute-forces all possible values for the unknown private attribute and observes the target model's loss, outputting the value for which the loss is closest to the target's expected training loss. Since there are no attributes in our data sets that are explicitly annotated as private, we randomly choose five attributes, and perform the attribute inference attack on each attribute independently, and report the averaged results.
new_text: Yeom et al.’s <cit.> attack framework offers a more straightforward approach compared to Shokri et al.’s design. It assumes a white-box attacker who has access to both the target model and its expected training loss on the private dataset. For membership inference, the attacker observes the target model’s loss on the input record and classifies it as a member of the private dataset if the loss is smaller than the expected training loss; otherwise, the record is labeled a non-member. The same principle applies to attribute inference: given an input record, the attacker brute-forces all possible values for the unknown private attribute, observes the target model’s loss for each, and outputs the value associated with the loss closest to the expected training loss. Because our datasets lack explicitly annotated private attributes, we randomly selected five attributes, conducted the attribute inference attack independently on each, and reported the averaged results.

For instance, at ε = 5.0, zCDP records 1 loss at 5%, and RDP matches this, whereas Advanced Composition remains stable with no 5% losses. The most significant divergence occurs at ε = 50.0 and 100.0, where FPRs drop sharply (e.g., Naive Composition’s FPR falls from 0.92 to 0.89 at ε=100), and loss counts rise substantially. Here, zCDP and RDP show comparable performance, with losses ranging from 6–28 at 1% and 12–67 at 5%. Notably, Naive Composition’s 5% losses exceed 41 at ε=100, reflecting its weaker calibration. At ε=1000.0, all methods converge to FPRs below 0.11, with losses in the hundreds, underscoring the trade-off between privacy and data utility at high ε. These trends highlight how each mechanism balances accuracy and privacy, with zCDP and RDP demonstrating more consistent performance at mid-range ε compared to Naive and Advanced Composition.

Recently, some NLP systems have exploited visual features to capture visual relationships among characters in compositional writing systems such as Chinese or Korean <cit.>.
However, in more general cases, current neural NLP systems have no notion of visual character similarity.
Rather, they either treat characters as discrete units
forming a word
or
they represent characters by randomly initialized embeddings and update them during training—typically in order to generate a character-based word representation that is robust to morphological variation or spelling mistakes <cit.>.
Intriguingly, this marked distinction between human and machine processing can be exploited as a blind spot of NLP systems.
For example, spammers might send malicious
emails or post toxic comments to online discussion forums <cit.> by visually `perturbing' the input text in such a way that it is still easily recoverable by humans.
new_text: Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have seen systems incorporate visual features to model character-level relationships in cursive or character-based scripts like Chinese or Korean <cit.>. However, in most scenarios, contemporary neural NLP models lack an inherent understanding of visual character similarity. Instead, they either treat characters as atomic units that compose words or encode characters using randomly initialized embeddings updated through training—primarily to create robust representations that accommodate morphological variations or spelling errors <cit.>. Strikingly, this stark contrast in how humans and machines process text—where humans perceive visual similarity while models rely on learned patterns—introduces potential vulnerabilities. Malicious actors could exploit this by crafting adversarial inputs, such as visually altered text in emails or online forums, that retain readability for humans but evade detection by automated systems <cit.>.

old_text: In this paper, we proposed a trilinear attention sampling network for fine-grained image recognition, which can learn rich feature representations from hundreds of part proposals. Instead of ensembling multiple part CNNs, we adopted knowledge distilling method to integrate fine-grained features into a single stream, which is not only efficient but also effective. Extensive experiments in CUB-Bird, iNaturalist 2017 and Stanford-Car demonstrate that TASN is able to outperform part-ensemble models even with a single stream. In the future, we will further study the proposed TASN in the following directions: 1) attention selection strategy, i.e., learning to select which details should be learned and distilled instead of randomly selecting, 2) conduct attention-based sampling over convolutional features instead of only over images, and 3) extend our work to other vision tasks, e.g., object detection and segmentation.
new_text: In this paper, we propose a trilinear attention sampling network (TASN) designed for fine-grained image recognition, aiming to efficiently capture detailed visual patterns critical for distinguishing subtle class differences. To achieve this, TASN learns discriminative feature representations by analyzing hundreds of part proposals—local image regions that highlight potential areas of variation. These part-level features are typically extracted using multiple specialized convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a process that, while effective, becomes computationally expensive when ensembled. Instead, we adopt knowledge distillation to consolidate fine-grained information into a single streamlined model. This approach not only reduces computational overhead compared to ensembling but also maintains high accuracy, as demonstrated through experiments on benchmark datasets. Comprehensive evaluations on CUB-Bird, iNaturalist 2017, and Stanford-Car datasets confirm that TASN outperforms traditional part-ensemble models despite operating with a single network stream, highlighting the effectiveness of its attention-driven knowledge integration. Looking ahead, we aim to enhance TASN in three directions: first, developing a more adaptive attention selection strategy to systematically determine which specific visual details are critical for learning, rather than relying on random sampling; second, extending attention-based feature sampling to convolutional feature maps, enabling the model to focus on both spatial and hierarchical patterns; and third, exploring the application of TASN to broader vision tasks such as object detection and segmentation, where localized attention mechanisms may offer similar efficiency advantages.

old_text: We have presented an online method to learn a part-based dictionary representation of an image dataset, designed for accurate and efficient approximations of morphological operators. This method relies on auto-encoder networks, with a deep encoder for a higher reconstruction capability and a shallow linear decoder for a better interpretation of the representation. Among the online part-based methods using auto-encoders, it achieves the state-of-the-art trade-off between the accuracy of reconstructions and the sparsity of image encodings. Moreover, it ensures a strict (that is, non approximated) non-negativity of the learned representation. We especially evaluated the learned representation on an additional criterion, that is the commutation of the representation with a morphological dilation, and noted that all online methods perform worse than the offline sparse-NMF algorithm. A possible improvement would be to impose a major sparsity to the dictionary images an appropriate regularization. Additionally, using a morphological layer <cit.> as a decoder may be more consistent with our definition of part-based approximation, since a representation in the (max, +) algebra would commute with the morphological dilation by essence.
new_text: We have developed an online method to learn a part-based dictionary representation from an image dataset. This approach is specifically designed to enable accurate and efficient approximations of morphological operators, which are essential in image processing for tasks like segmentation and feature extraction. The method employs auto-encoder networks, where the deep encoder is designed to enhance reconstruction accuracy by capturing complex features, while the shallow linear decoder ensures the learned representation remains interpretable and structured. Among online part-based methods utilizing auto-encoders, our approach strikes the best balance between the fidelity of reconstructed images and the sparsity of their encoded representations. Additionally, the method enforces strict non-negativity in the learned representations, meaning the resulting dictionary elements are strictly positive and non-approximated, which is crucial for certain applications. To further assess the representation’s properties, we evaluated how well it commutes with morphological dilation, a key operation in morphological processing. Our findings indicate that all online methods, including ours, underperform compared to the offline sparse-NMF algorithm in this criterion. Potential enhancements include applying a stronger sparsity constraint through regularization techniques to refine the dictionary elements. Furthermore, incorporating a morphological layer as a decoder could align better with the part-based approximation framework. This is because representations in the (max, +) algebra inherently commute with morphological operations like dilation, which would make the model’s behavior more mathematically consistent with its intended applications.

old_text: To teach our agent complex sequences of action in a sparse reward setup, we note that it is easier to learn how to reach nearby goals than further ones. This defines the DtD method: in order to train the low-level agent in an efficient manner, for a given starting point (o_0, ag_0, g) ∈𝒪×𝒢×𝒢 in an episode, π_1 (i.e. high-level agent) first generates sub-goals that are in the vicinity of ag_0. This is done by making the first sub-goal sg_1 be a noisy perturbation of ag_0, formally: sg_0 = ag_0+𝒩(0,σ), with 𝒩 a Gaussian distribution and σ the noise parameter, effectively ignoring the final goal g. Doing so, the low-level policy π_0 can be trained easily on reaching these newly defined sub-goals. The other central idea of DtD is to ignore whether or not goals and sub-goals have been achieved during an episode, and to use HER for both π_0 and π_1 to extract as much information as possible from past experience.
new_text: To teach complex action sequences in sparse reward environments, we leverage the fact that nearby goals are easier to learn than distant ones, forming the basis of our DtD method. The high-level policy π₁ generates sub-goals (sg₁) as noisy perturbations of the initial goal ag₀, defined as sg₁ = ag₀ + 𝒩(0,σ), where 𝒩 is a Gaussian distribution with noise parameter σ. This local sub-goal strategy enables efficient training of the low-level policy π₀, decoupling sub-goal pursuit from the final goal g. DtD further optimizes learning by omitting success checks for sub-goals and applying hindsight experience replay (HER) to both π₀ and π₁, maximizing information extraction from historical episodes.

new_text: The N2NMN<cit.> and PG+EE<cit.> approaches involve the artificial design of modules to address specific sub-problems, where a layout is learned from the input question to assemble question-relevant modules for answer prediction. A key limitation of these methods is their reliance on predefined modules, which must be tailored to the dataset or supplemented with additional supervision signals during training. For instance, the CLEVER dataset provides ground truth programs explicitly encoding the compositional reasoning steps needed to answer questions, highlighting the necessity of such annotated data for these methods.

old_text: Robotic systems are ever more capable of automation and fulfilment of complex tasks, particularly with reliance on recent advances in intelligent systems, deep learning and artificial intelligence in general. However, as robots and humans come closer together in their interactions, the matter of interpretability, or explainability of robot decision-making processes for the human grows in importance. A successful interaction and collaboration would only be possible through mutual understanding of underlying representations of the environment and the task at hand. This is currently a challenge in deep learning systems. We present a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning system, consisting of a low-level agent handling the large actions/states space of a robotic system efficiently, by following the directives of a high-level agent which is learning the high-level dynamics of the environment and task. This high-level agent forms a representation of the world and task at hand that is interpretable for a human operator. The method, which we call Dot-to-Dot, is tested on a MuJoCo-based model of the Fetch Robotics Manipulator, as well as a Shadow Hand, to test its performance. Results show efficient learning of complex actions/states spaces by the low-level agent, and an interpretable representation of the task and decision-making process learned by the high-level agent.
new_text: Robotic systems are increasingly capable of automation and executing complex tasks, particularly through the integration of recent advances in intelligent systems, deep learning, and artificial intelligence. As robots and humans engage more closely in collaborative tasks, the interpretability—or explainability—of robot decision-making processes becomes critical for effective human-robot interaction. Achieving successful collaboration requires mutual understanding of the underlying representations of the environment and the specific task at hand, a challenge inherent to deep learning systems due to their opaque nature. To address this, we propose a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning framework comprising a low-level agent and a high-level agent. The low-level agent efficiently navigates the large action/state space of the robotic system by executing instructions from the high-level agent, which models the high-level dynamics of the environment and task. Crucially, the high-level agent generates a task representation that is interpretable to human operators. Dubbed Dot-to-Dot, this method is evaluated on a MuJoCo-based Fetch Robotics Manipulator model and a Shadow Hand. Experimental results demonstrate the low-level agent’s ability to efficiently master complex action/state spaces, while the high-level agent acquires an interpretable representation of the task and its decision-making process.

old_text: In figure <ref>, we show the two extremes in terms of distance from the initial state to the end-goal. The `FetchPush` environment is ideal to look at inner representations as it is almost two dimensional (goals are always on the tabletop). Figure <ref> shows this setup. We first look at the Q-values at the very beginning of training, after just one epoch, as shown in figure <ref>. We can see the values are very close to each other and spread in a small interval, which shows that the high-level agent does not have a clear representation of the environment yet. Despite this lack of clear representation, the agent seems to attribute higher values to sub-goals closer to the end-goal (to the right of the table) rather than those close to the starting position (to its left). This makes sense as sub-goals close to the end-goal are most likely to allow the agent to reach its destination, and are therefore the very first sub-goals that lead to successful traces. Finally, after training, the best policy's Q-values are represented in figure <ref>. We can now see that the values are spread over a much larger interval, and therefore the higher values mean the associated sub-goals are clearly better candidates. This area of higher value is located well in the middle between the starting position and the end-goal. Note that in practice, the sub-goal will only be the point with the highest value on this heatmap. We can therefore conclude that the agent learnt a good representation of its environment as well as a notion of distance, considering the effects of friction and the dynamics involved in pushing a block around to an end-goal.
new_text: In figure <ref>, we examine the extreme ends of the distance spectrum between the initial state and the end-goal. The `FetchPush` environment is particularly suited for analyzing internal representations due to its near-two-dimensional nature (goals are consistently placed on the tabletop), as illustrated in figure <ref>. Initially, during the first epoch of training (shown in figure <ref>), Q-values are tightly clustered within a narrow range, indicating the high-level agent has not yet developed a distinct environmental representation. However, even in this early phase, the agent assigns marginally higher Q-values to sub-goals proximate to the end-goal (right side of the table) compared to those near the starting position (left side). This reflects an implicit prioritization of sub-goals closer to the target, as these are most likely to yield successful trajectories. After full training, the optimal policy's Q-values (figure <ref>) span a significantly broader range, with higher values concentrated in the central region between the start and end-goal. Notably, the selected sub-goal corresponds to the heatmap’s peak value. This demonstrates that the agent has learned both a robust environmental representation and a functional understanding of distance, accounting for physical constraints like friction and the kinematic challenges of block manipulation.

old_text: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a common retinal disease that leads to blindness. For diagnosis purposes, DR image grading aims to provide automatic DR grade classification, which is not addressed in conventional research methods of binary DR image classification. Small objects in the eye images, like lesions and microaneurysms, are essential to DR grading in medical imaging, but they could easily be influenced by other objects. To address these challenges, we propose a new deep learning architecture, called BiRA-Net, which combines the attention model for feature extraction and bilinear model for fine-grained classification. Furthermore, in considering the distance between different grades of different DR categories, we propose a new loss function, called grading loss, which leads to improved training convergence of the proposed approach. Experimental results are provided to demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed approach.
new_text: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a prevalent retinal disease that can lead to blindness. While traditional research focuses on binary classification of DR images, DR image grading aims to automate the classification of severity grades—a task not adequately addressed by conventional methods. Small diagnostic features in retinal images, such as lesions and microaneurysms, are critical for accurate grading but are often affected by surrounding structures. To address these challenges, we propose BiRA-Net, a novel deep learning architecture that incorporates an attention model for feature extraction and a bilinear model for fine-grained classification. Additionally, by accounting for inter-grade distances across DR severity categories, we introduce a new loss function, termed grading loss, which enhances the model's training convergence. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed approach.

For the high-level vision, flight planning, and control tasks, we utilize a lightweight smart camera called Jevois (weighing just 17g), which is powered by a quad-core ARM Cortex A7 processor and a dual-core Mali-400 GPU. These hardware specifications enable efficient real-time processing, making Jevois well-suited for the computational demands of our application. In our experimental setup, two distinct threads operate concurrently on the Jevois platform. The first thread is dedicated to vision detection, specifically identifying gates in the environment, while the second thread focuses on filtering sensory data and computing control commands to stabilize and direct the system (see Figure <ref>). This division of labor allows the system to perform specialized tasks at optimal frequencies: the gate detection thread runs at 10–30 Hz, balancing responsiveness with computational efficiency, while the filtering and control thread operates at a much higher frequency of 512 Hz, ensuring rapid and precise adjustments to the system's behavior. 

The vision detection thread processes image data sequentially, analyzing each frame to detect the presence of gates. Upon successful detection, it triggers a signal to notify the control thread of the event. The control thread continuously predicts the system’s dynamic states and calculates necessary control commands at its high frequency. However, it only initiates parameter estimation via data fitting once it has both received a gate detection signal and accumulated a sufficient number of data points within a predefined time window. This two-stage approach ensures that the system only processes relevant data when necessary, minimizing computational overhead while maintaining accuracy. Importantly, the control algorithm itself remains consistent with the methodology detailed in Section <ref>, reinforcing the system’s reliability and coherence.

Neuromorphic processing can benefit from photonics in three major ways. First, photonics can significantly reduce the amount of energy consumed in interconnects among PEs by avoiding energy dissipation due to charging and discharging of electrical wires. Secondly, current neuromorphic algorithms known to neural networks and in particular in CNNs heavily rely on multiply and accumulate (MAC) operation, which can be realized with very low energy budgets in photonics compared to its electronic counterpart. Finally, photonics can increase communication and computation bandwidth by exploiting WDM. WDM allow for higher density computation and communication between PEs by packing more channels and parallel computations in a neuromorphic processor.
new_text: Photonics offer three primary advantages for enhancing neuromorphic processing. First, photonics minimize energy consumption in interconnects between processing elements (PEs) by eliminating the energy loss associated with electrical wire charging and discharging. Second, modern neuromorphic algorithms, especially those in convolutional neural networks (CNNs), depend on multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, which photonic implementations can perform at significantly lower energy costs compared to electronic systems. Finally, photonics enhance computational and communication bandwidth through wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM), enabling higher data density by supporting multiple parallel channels between PEs.

Notations: To distinguish vectors and matrices from scalars, we use boldfaced characters throughout the paper. For clarity, when a matrix is denoted by **M**, the expressions **M**(m,·), **M**(·,m), and **M**(m,n) explicitly refer to its m-th row (all elements in row m), m-th column (all elements in column m), and the individual element at the (m,n) position, respectively. Similarly, the vector (x₁,…,xₙ) can be abbreviated as (xᵢ)ₙ₁ or simply (xᵢ) when the index set is unambiguous from the context. The i-th entry of a vector **x** is denoted as **x**(i). In standard notation, the symbol **1** represents a column vector whose components are all ones, while **I** denotes the identity matrix, whose diagonal entries are ones and off-diagonal entries are zeros. 

Probability distributions are represented using the parameters provided: the categorical distribution with probabilities p₁,…,pₖ is written as p₁,…,pₖ, and the normal distribution with mean vector **μ** and covariance matrix **Σ** is denoted as **μΣ**. The symbol ∼ is used to indicate that two random variables share the same distribution. Conditional relationships are expressed with **y**|**x**, representing a random variable **y** given the value of **x**, and the conditional probability density is denoted by p(**y**|**x**). The symbol E represents the expectation operator, while E_q specifies expectation taken with respect to the distribution q. 

To simplify expressions, we employ the indicator function **I**(a,b), which outputs 1 if a equals b and 0 otherwise, and the cardinality notation |𝒮|, which gives the number of elements in the set 𝒮. The vectorized form of a matrix **M**, where its columns are concatenated into a single column vector, is denoted as **vec**(M). Additionally, **x** may represent a one-hot encoding of x in a finite set; this representation, which has a single 1 at the index corresponding to x and 0 elsewhere, is defined implicitly based on the context of the problem.

new_text: Active learning <cit.> involves utilizing a pool of unlabeled images or videos to train a high-accuracy visual model while strategically minimizing the labeling effort by iteratively selecting the most informative training samples. This differs from passive learning, where training data is randomly sampled without such strategic selection, ultimately demanding a larger labeling budget to achieve comparable results.

The supervision consists in modifying the original visual data (e.g. a set of images) according to known transforms (e.g. image rotations <cit.>), training the pretext CNN to predict such transforms; thus, the transforms are the labels/supervision for the pretext task. A typical aggregation workload involves grouping tuples by a designated grouping column and then applying an aggregate function to each group. Aggregate functions are divided into three categories: distributive, algebraic, and holistic. Distributive functions, such as the Count function used in W2 (see Table <ref>), can be decomposed and processed in a distributed manner. This means that the input can be split up, processed, and recombined to produce the final result. Algebraic functions combine two or more distributive functions. For instance, Average can be broken down into two distributive functions: Count and Sum. Holistic aggregate functions, such as the Median function used in W1, cannot be decomposed into multiple functions or steps. These aggregate functions do not produce intermediate values, and each output tuple is the result of processing all of the input tuples for its corresponding group. As a result, these aggregate functions are more demanding on the memory system. W3 represents a hash join query. As described in <cit.>, the query joins two tables with a size ratio of 1:16, which is designed to mimic common decision support systems. The join is performed by building a hash table on the smaller table, and probing the larger table for matching keys. W4 is an index nested loop join using the same dataset as W3. The main difference between W3 and W4 is that W3 builds an ad hoc hash table to perform the join, whereas W4 uses a pre-built in-memory index that accelerates lookups to one of the relations. W5 is a database system workload, using the queries and datasets from the TPC-H benchmark <cit.>. We evaluate W5 on two database systems: MonetDB <cit.> and PostgreSQL <cit.>.

To ensure fair results, we clear the page cache before running the workload and report the average runtime, after disregarding the first (cold) run. In a similar vein to the other experiments, we evaluated the impact of the operating system configuration, memory placement policies, and memory allocators. First we ran all 22 TPC-H queries, and calculated the query latency reduction caused by disabling AutoNUMA and THP, compared to the system default. The results depicted in Figure <ref> show that MonetDB's query latencies improved between 2% and 43%, with an average improvement of 14.5%. The results for PostgreSQL are less impressive, with an average improvement of 3% and five queries taking longer to complete. We believe this is due to PostGreSQL's rigid multi-process query processing approach. Next we evaluate the effect of memory allocator overriding on MonetDB. To do so, we selected queries 5 and 18 due to their usage of both joins and aggregation. The results shown in Figure <ref> indicate that tbbmalloc can provide an average query latency reduction of up to 12% for Query 5, and 20% for Query 18, compared to ptmalloc.
new_text: Assessing NUMA-related impacts on databases such as MonetDB and PostgreSQL is more complex than with synthetic workloads, as these systems load data from disk on demand rather than maintaining all data in memory. To ensure consistent evaluation, the page cache was cleared prior to each workload execution, and average runtimes were measured after excluding the initial (cold) run. Similar to prior experiments, the influence of OS configurations, memory placement policies, and memory allocators was analyzed. The 22 TPC-H queries were executed, and the latency improvements from disabling AutoNUMA and THP were compared to default system settings. As illustrated in Figure <ref>, MonetDB demonstrated latency reductions ranging from 2% to 43%, with an average of 14.5%. Conversely, PostgreSQL showed smaller gains (3% average), with five queries exhibiting increased execution times, likely due to its rigid multi-process architecture. For MonetDB, memory allocator performance was tested using queries 5 and 18, which involve joins and aggregations. Data in Figure <ref> reveals that tbbmalloc outperformed ptmalloc, achieving 12% and 20% latency reductions for Query 5 and 18, respectively.

old_text: We now describe a multi-threaded microbenchmark that we use to gain insight on the relative performance of these memory allocators. The goal of the microbenchmark is to answer the question: how well do these allocators scale up on a NUMA machine? This experiment simulates a memory-intensive workload with multiple threads utilizing the allocator at the same time. Each thread completes 100 million memory operations, consisting of allocating memory and writing to it, or reading an existing item and then deallocating it. The distribution of allocation sizes is inversely proportional to the size class (smaller allocations are more frequent). We use two metrics to compare the allocators: execution time, and memory allocation overhead. The execution time gives an idea of how fast an allocator is, as well as its efficiency when being used in a NUMA system by concurrent threads. In Figure <ref>, we vary the number of threads in order to see how each allocator behaves under contention. The results show that tcmalloc provides the fastest single-threaded performance, but falls behind as the number of threads is increased. Hoard and tbbmalloc show good scalability, and outperform the other allocators by a considerable margin. In Figure <ref>, we show each allocator's overhead. This is calculated by measuring the amount of memory allocated by the operating system (as maximum resident set size), and dividing it by the amount of memory that was requested by the microbenchmark. This experiment shows considerably higher memory overhead for mcmalloc as the number of threads increases. Hoard and tbbmalloc are slightly more memory hungry than the other allocators. Based on these results, we omit supermalloc and mcmalloc from subsequent experiments, due to their poor performance in terms of scalability and memory overhead respectively.

To obtain a pre-selected pool of images meeting the specified criteria, we implement a greedy sampling strategy applied on a per-country basis. First, the proportion of target images allocated to each country is determined by combining two factors: the number of available images in that country and its population, both weighted by a predefined global distribution (20% for North America, 20% for Europe, 20% for Asia, 15% for South America, 15% for Oceania, and 10% for Africa). This weighting ensures representation from all continents while adjusting for disparities in data availability and population size.  

Next, to ensure diverse geographical coverage within each country, we uniformly divide sampled images into spatial bins based on their geographical coordinates. Random images are then selected from each bin, guaranteeing that both rural and urban areas are adequately represented. In the final step of the greedy sampling process, we prioritize images that contain at least one traffic sign, as identified by the Mapillary API. This step helps focus the dataset on relevant traffic-related content. Additionally, we ensure variation in image characteristics by including images with different resolutions, camera manufacturers, and scene properties (details on defining scene properties are provided in the supplementary materials). To further enhance dataset diversity, a distance constraint is applied to ensure that selected images are sufficiently geographically separated, reducing the risk of including highly correlated images or redundant traffic sign instances.

section: Idea 6: Compact encoding of the ancestors

The remaining log^2n term comes from the list of Θ(log n) ancestor identifiers that each node holds.
Note that it is crucial to have some way of naming these ancestors, such that two neighbors of the graph can decide which anchor of their lists they should use to compute the max value, and then check the cycle property.
Also, in general, there is no better way of naming a set of Θ(log n) nodes than to use Θ(log^2n) bits.
But, the sets of nodes we are interested in are not arbitrary: they are chains of nodes that form a path from a node to the root, through all its ancestors.
We can tweak the names such that retrieving the concatenation of names of such chains requires small labels.
new_text: The remaining log² n term derives from the list of Θ(log n) ancestor identifiers that each node holds. It is crucial to have a method for naming these ancestors so that adjacent graph nodes can determine which entry in their respective lists to use when computing the maximum value and verifying the cycle property. In general, no more efficient way exists to identify a set of Θ(log n) nodes than by using Θ(log² n) bits. However, the node sets we consider are not arbitrary: they are paths from a node to the root, traversing its entire ancestry. By adjusting the labeling scheme, the concatenation of names along such paths can be represented with compact labels.

First, PCD-by-PCD employs the MMPC algorithm <cit.> for PC discovery, while CMB relies on HINTON-MB <cit.> for orientation. However, MMHC requires exhaustive subset searches to identify the PC set of a given variable, and HINTON-MB necessitates finding the PC set for each variable within the target’s PC set, leading to excessive computational time for PC/MB set identification. Second, both methods struggle to resolve direct causal relationships efficiently. For instance, in a triangular structure (Fig.<ref>), where T directly causes A and B, and A further causes B, PCD-by-PCD cannot determine T’s direct effects from PCD(T), requiring additional searches. Similarly, even with V-structures involving T and B, CMB fails to orient edges between T and variables B, L, E, and J using only T’s MB. This forces CMB to repeatedly compute MBs for other variables to infer relationships. Can direct causal identification for a target variable T be accelerated?

old_text: * We provide a novel viewpoint for learning local causal structure of a given variable by identifying several parents and more children of a given variable with the help of EOMB, and propose a new local causal structure discovery algorithm, called ELCD. ELCD utilizes the proposed EOMB algorithm to efficiently determine direct causes and effects of a given variable. In this way, ELCD can reduce the searching scope in looking for direct causes and effects of a given variable T and achieve satisfying performance.
new_text: By leveraging the proposed EOMB algorithm, we introduce a novel framework for uncovering the local causal structure of a target variable T. Specifically, the EOMB method enables the identification of multiple parent variables and a broader set of child variables, which directly informs the causal relationships involving T. Building on this, we present a new local causal discovery algorithm called ELCD. The ELCD algorithm systematically integrates EOMB to pinpoint direct causes and effects of T by iteratively narrowing the search space for potential causal connections. This targeted approach reduces the complexity of exploring exhaustive combinations of variables, thereby enhancing the efficiency of the discovery process. The reduction in search scope not only streamlines computational efforts but also ensures ELCD achieves robust and practical performance in identifying local causal structures.

The performances of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are usually evaluated by the metric word error rate (WER) when the manually transcribed data are provided, which are, however, expensively available in the real scenario.
In addition, the empirical distribution of WER for most ASR systems usually tends to put a significant mass near zero, making it difficult to simulate with a single continuous distribution.
In order to address the two issues of ASR quality estimation (QE), we propose a novel neural zero-inflated model to predict the WER of the ASR result without transcripts.
We design a neural zero-inflated beta regression on top of a bidirectional transformer language model conditional on speech features (speech-BERT).
We adopt the pre-training strategy of token level mask language modeling for speech-BERT as well, and further fine-tune with our zero-inflated layer for the mixture of discrete and continuous outputs.
The experimental results show that our approach achieves better performance on WER prediction in the metrics of Pearson and MAE, compared with most existed quality estimation algorithms for ASR or machine translation.
new_text: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) system performance is typically evaluated using word error rate (WER), though manually transcribed data—scarce in real-world scenarios—limit this approach. Additionally, WER distributions for most ASR systems often concentrate near zero, challenging representation by a single continuous distribution. To address these issues in ASR quality estimation (QE), we propose a neural zero-inflated model to predict WER without transcriptions. Our architecture combines a bidirectional transformer language model (speech-BERT) with a zero-inflated beta regression layer. We pre-train speech-BERT using token-level masked language modeling and fine-tune it with the zero-inflated layer to handle discrete-continuous output mixtures. Experimental results demonstrate superior WER prediction in Pearson and MAE metrics compared to existing ASR or machine translation quality estimation methods.

This paper introduces a novel semi-supervised training methodology for monocular depth estimation, that both improves on the current state of the art and is also more robust to the presence of sparse labels. To accomplish this, we propose a new supervised loss term that operates in the image space, and thus is compatible with the widely used photometric loss in the semi-supervised setting.
We show, using the popular KITTI benchmark, that our proposed methodology can efficiently incorporate information from depth labels into pretrained self-supervised models, allowing them to produce metrically accurate estimates while further improving the overall quality of resulting depth maps. Further analysis also indicates that our model presents a strong robustness to the degradation of available supervised labels, reaching results competitive with the current state-of-the-art even when as few as 4 beams are considered at training time. Future work will focus on the scalability of the proposed semi-supervised training methodology, investigating its application to different datasets, sources of labeled information and robustness to domain transfer.

Our approach builds on prior work in controllable text generation <cit.>, in which a Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) model is adapted to regulate attributes of the generated text. We apply this framework to SS by incorporating attributes relevant to simplified sentences, including output length, degree of paraphrasing, lexical complexity, and syntactic complexity. Dense depth estimation from a single image is a key problem in computer vision, with exciting applications in a multitude of robotic tasks. Initially viewed as a direct regression problem, requiring annotated labels as supervision at training time, in the past few years a substantial amount of work has been done in self-supervised depth training based on strong geometric cues, both from stereo cameras and more recently from monocular video sequences.
In this paper we investigate how these two approaches (supervised & self-supervised) can be effectively combined, so that a depth model can learn to encode true scale from sparse supervision while achieving high fidelity local accuracy by leveraging geometric cues. To this end, we propose a novel supervised loss term that complements the widely used photometric loss, and show how it can be used to train robust semi-supervised monocular depth estimation models.
Furthermore, we evaluate how much supervision is actually necessary to train accurate scale-aware monocular depth models, showing that with our proposed framework, very sparse LiDAR information, with as few as 4 beams (less than 100 valid depth values per image), is enough to achieve results competitive with the current state-of-the-art.
new_text: Single-image dense depth estimation represents a foundational challenge in computer vision, with significant applications across diverse robotic tasks. Initially framed as a regression problem dependent on annotated labels for training supervision, recent advances have shifted toward self-supervised methods that exploit geometric constraints derived from stereo systems and, increasingly, monocular video sequences. This paper examines the synergistic integration of supervised and self-supervised paradigms, aiming to enable depth models to simultaneously acquire accurate global scale from minimal labeled data and refine local detail through geometric reasoning. To achieve this, we introduce a novel supervised loss component that augments the commonly adopted photometric loss, demonstrating its effectiveness in training resilient semi-supervised monocular depth estimation architectures. Additionally, we quantify the minimum supervisory requirements for scale-aware monocular depth models, revealing that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance with exceptionally sparse LiDAR supervision—specifically, just 4 beams (fewer than 100 valid depth measurements per image).

There are a number of promising avenues for future research. The first is the untapped source of architecture inspiration that can be drawn from further study of insect brains. Insects face tremendous pressure to minimize neural costs for metabolic reasons <cit.>; they have to have the most efficient brains possible <cit.>. For example, there is a small recurrent pathway in the honey bee mushroom body called the protocerebral calycal tract. In hybrid ASR <cit.>, an acoustic encoder is used to encode an input sequence x_1, ⋯, x_T to a sequence of high level embedding vectors z_1, ⋯, z_T. These embedding vectors are used to produce a posterior distribution of tied states of hidden Markov model (HMM), such as senone <cit.> or chenone <cit.>, for each frame. These posterior distributions are then combined with other knowledge sources such as lexicons and LMs to construct a search graph. A decoder is then used to find the best hypothesis. Different neural networks can be used as the encoder: in DNN, TDNN and CNN, z_t is a function of x_t and its fixed number of neighboring frames; in uni-directional RNNs, z_t is a function of x_1 to x_t, while in bi-directional RNNs, z_t is a function of the entire input sequence.

In the first proposed algorithm, the adjacent nodes having the same value form a set called spot. Afterwards, the spots with majority value try to corrode the spots with non-majority values.
The second proposed algorithm is based on pairwise interactions between nodes.
The proposed algorithms have a termination detection procedure to check whether voting is achieved.
We show that the probability of success of the first algorithm goes to one as the percentage of nodes choosing the majority vote as their initial values gets close to one. The second algorithm returns the correct vote with high probability. Our experiments show that the algorithms are fairly invariant to the network topology, initial distribution of values, and network size.
new_text: In this paper, we propose two distributed algorithms, named Distributed Voting with Beeps (DVB), for multi-choice voting in the beep model, where each node can communicate with its neighbors solely by sending beep signals. The two algorithms feature simple structures and are suitable for networks with severe constraints on message size. The first algorithm operates by grouping adjacent nodes with the same value into a set termed a "spot," followed by spots with a majority value attempting to erode non-majority spots. The second algorithm relies on pairwise interactions between nodes. Both algorithms incorporate a termination detection procedure to verify whether voting has been achieved. We prove that the success probability of the first algorithm approaches one as the proportion of nodes initially selecting the majority value approaches one. The second algorithm accurately identifies the correct vote with high probability. Experiments demonstrate that the algorithms remain largely invariant to variations in network topology, initial value distributions, and network size.

We propose two complementary discourse graphs to further enhance the model: (i) an RST Graph derived from rhetorical structure theory (RST) discourse trees, and (ii) a Coreference Graph mapping coreference mentions within the document. We define the image crossover operation as copying parts from a source image y into a target image x and blending the boundaries.
As initialization, we embed the target image x to obtain the W^+ code w^*. We then perform masked W^+ optimization (W_l) with blurred masks M_blur to embed the regions in x and y that contribute to the final image. Blurred masks are obtained by convolution of the binary mask with a Gaussian filter of suitable size. Then, we perform noise optimization. Details are provided in Alg. <ref>.
new_text: The image crossover operation involves transferring elements from a source image *y* into a target image *x* while ensuring a seamless transition at their boundaries. To begin, the target image *x* is embedded into a latent space to generate the *W^+* code *w^*, which encodes the image's structural characteristics. Next, a masked *W^+* optimization is performed using blurred masks *M_blur* to integrate the relevant regions from *x* and *y* into the composite image. These blurred masks are created by convolving a binary mask with a Gaussian filter of appropriate size, a technique that softens abrupt edges and enables smoother blending of the transferred content. This step ensures that the selected regions from the source and target images align effectively within the latent representation. After this, a separate noise optimization refines the generated image, adjusting residual artifacts or inconsistencies to improve overall quality. Algorithmic details are described in Alg. <ref>.

old_text: In this work, we propose an Adversarial Neural Architecture Search method to address the above challenges, which we term AdversarialNAS (Fig. <ref> c)). We relax the search space to be continuous. Thus the architecture can be represented by a probability distribution and searched in a differentiable manner. First, we propose to directly utilize the discriminator to evaluate the architecture of generator in each searching iteration. Specifically, when searching for the architecture of a generator, the discriminator would provide the supervision signal with an adversarial loss, which is utilized to update the architecture distribution of generator through gradient descent. The extra computation cost of Inception Score is abundant. Thus our method is much more efficient. Second, in order to consider the relevance and balance between the generator and discriminator, we propose to search the discriminator simultaneously. Specifically, we adopt the generator to evaluate the architecture of discriminator and use the adversarial loss from generator to update the architecture of discriminator through gradient descent. The two architectures play against each other in a competition to continually improve performance for both of them, which is essentially an adversarial searching mechanism. Therefore, the designed searching methods gets rid of the extra evaluation metric and solves the weakly supervision task through an adversarial mechanism. It adequately considers the relevance and balance between the two architectures, thus can search for a superior generator.
new_text: This paper introduces an Adversarial Neural Architecture Search approach, termed AdversarialNAS (Fig. <ref> c)), to tackle the aforementioned challenges by transforming the search space into a continuous domain. The architecture is then modeled as a probability distribution, enabling differentiable search. First, we leverage the discriminator to assess the generator’s architecture during each search iteration by utilizing adversarial loss, which guides gradient descent updates to refine the generator’s architecture distribution. This eliminates the high computational burden of metrics like Inception Score, significantly improving efficiency. Second, to maintain harmony and balance between the generator and discriminator, we simultaneously optimize the discriminator’s architecture. The generator evaluates the discriminator’s design, and adversarial loss from the generator drives gradient-based updates to the discriminator. Through this competitive interplay, both architectures iteratively enhance their performance, forming an adversarial search framework. This method removes reliance on auxiliary evaluation metrics and resolves weakly supervised tasks via adversarial learning. By explicitly considering the interdependence and equilibrium between the two components, it effectively identifies a superior generator.

old_text: High-end wearable systems are expensive and provide low comfort for the users, which limit their wide range application. Recently, smart bands and smartwatches became adopted by consumers. These devices are equipped with a rich set of sensors such as accelerometer, heart rate monitor and skin conductance. These advances create an opportunity to build a continuous implicit authentication system. However, these devices are prune to activity related errors <cit.> unlike full lead ECG systems. Modality specific artifact detection and removal mechanism should be developed for accurate measurements. A solution suitable for IoT connected devices should be context-independent because every service may require different types of behavior. Therefore, systems that only work in certain scenarios such as while typing or walking are very limited in terms of the application area. new_text: Smartbands, often referred to as wristbands or smartwatches, are wearable devices designed for convenient attachment to the wrist or arm. As illustrated in Figure <ref>, these devices play a significant role in modern physiological monitoring. A notable advancement in smartband design is the extended battery life, which now typically lasts several days. For instance, the Empatica E4 model can operate continuously for two days even when all sensors are active <cit>. This improvement is critical for enabling prolonged data collection of physiological signals, as it reduces the need for frequent recharging during monitoring periods. Many smartbands incorporate photoplethysmography (PPG) sensors, which optically measure changes in blood volume within microvascular tissue <cit>. These PPG signals allow for the calculation of RR intervals—the time between consecutive heartbeats—which serve as a key indicator for heart rate variability analysis. Modern smartbands, such as Samsung Gear Series models, leverage APIs to expose RR interval data directly to users and applications. Samsung devices, for example, utilize the Tizen framework’s Human Activity Monitor API to retrieve this information. The PPG sampling frequencies vary across devices, ranging from 20Hz to 100Hz (e.g., 64Hz for the Empatica E4 and 100Hz for Samsung Gear models), which influences the granularity of data captured. To enhance accuracy in heartbeat detection, some devices employ cubic spline interpolation and use accelerometer data to filter out motion artifacts—a feature supported by both the Empatica and Tizen APIs <cit>. Additionally, smartbands are equipped with Bluetooth and near-field communication (NFC) capabilities, facilitating seamless connectivity to smartphones, edge computing systems, or cloud services. These wireless interfaces also enable contextual awareness, such as determining a user’s proximity to a computer or other devices.
