∙ Compromising a C&C Server: LNBot has a number of C&C servers each of which is controlling a mini botnet using a special software installed on them by the botmaster. As seen many times in the past, even the strongest botnets were taken down by legal authorities and cybersecurity researchers <cit.>. Therefore, it is highly likely that the mini botnets that are being run by C&C servers will be detected at some point in the future after starting their operations. Detection of a C&C server can result in the revelation of its location/IP address or even further the machine can be physically seized. In the latter case, adversaries would have access to the operating system, memory contents, logs, software etc. In LNBot, seizure of a C&C server does not reveal the botmaster or other C&C servers since a C&C server receive the commands through onion routed payments catered with Sphinx's mix-format which do not reveal their sender. Additionally, the communication between botmaster and C&C servers is 1-way meaning botmaster can talk to servers, but servers cannot talk to botmaster. This 1-way communication ensures that the identity of the botmaster will be kept secret at all times. In another scenario, where one of the bots on mini-botnets were detected and possibly seized, this could reveal the identity of the corresponding C&C server. As we explained above, such thing only can be used to shutdown the relevant mini botnet with no effect to the rest of the botnet. Even though taking down the C&C servers neither reveals the botmaster nor stops the botnet as a whole, it shuts down a part of the botnet resulting in less damage to victims.
new_text: Compromising a C&C Server: LNBot has a number of C&C servers, each of which controls a mini botnet using special software installed by the botmaster. As seen many times in the past, even the strongest botnets have been taken down by legal authorities and cybersecurity researchers <cit.>. Therefore, it is highly likely that the mini botnets managed by C&C servers will be detected at some point after they begin operations. Detection of a C&C server may result in the exposure of its location/IP address or the machine itself being physically seized. In the latter case, attackers could gain access to the operating system, memory contents, logs, software, etc. In LNBot, seizure of a C&C server does not reveal the botmaster or other C&C servers since each C&C server receives commands through onion-routed payments formatted with Sphinx’s mix format, which do not disclose the sender. Additionally, communication between the botmaster and C&C servers is one-way: the botmaster can send commands to servers, but servers cannot communicate with the botmaster. This one-way communication ensures the botmaster’s identity remains secret at all times. In another scenario, if one of the bots in a mini botnet is detected and possibly seized, this could reveal the identity of the corresponding C&C server. As explained above, such an event only permits shutdown of the relevant mini botnet with no impact on the rest of the botnet. Although taking down C&C servers neither exposes the botmaster nor halts the botnet as a whole, it disrupts a portion of the botnet, resulting in reduced damage to victims.

LN has been formed as a new payment network to address the drawbacks of Bitcoin transactions in terms of time and cost. In addition to anonymity, LN reduce the fees by performing off-chain transactions. This provides a perfect opportunity for covert communications as no transactions are recorded in the blockchain. Therefore, in this paper, we proposed a new covert hybrid botnet by utilizing the LN payment network formed for Bitcoin operations. The idea was to control the C&C servers through messages that are sent in the form of payments through the LN. Furthermore, we designed a novel one-to-many architecture for communication. The proof-of-concept implementation of this architecture indicated that LNBot can be successfully created and commands for attacks can be sent to C&C servers through LN with very high anonymity.
We have also shown that LNBot is resilient to the attacks assumed in our threat model.
new_text: LN was developed as a payment network to address Bitcoin's transaction latency and cost issues. By enabling off-chain transactions, LN reduces fees and enhances anonymity, facilitating covert communications since no transactions are recorded on the blockchain. This paper proposes a covert hybrid botnet leveraging LN for Bitcoin operations, using LN-based payments to control C&C servers. We designed a novel one-to-many communication architecture, with proof-of-concept implementation demonstrating LNBot's creation and the delivery of attack commands via LN with high anonymity. We further show LNBot's resilience against attacks in our threat model.

In a unicast a source sends information to a receiver and in a multicast a source sends information to several receivers. Typically, many such primitives are run simultaneously, causing these primitives to contend for the same resources, most notably the bandwidth of communication links.
new_text: Unicasts and multicasts represent fundamental and crucial information distribution mechanisms in contemporary communication networks. A unicast operation involves a source transmitting data to a single recipient, whereas a multicast operation involves a source transmitting data to multiple recipients. In practice, numerous instances of these mechanisms execute concurrently, leading to competition for shared resources, primarily the bandwidth capacity of communication links.

old_text: In this section, we compare the performances of different distributed computing schemes running on the heterogeneous Amazon cluster. In our experiments, we consider two scenarios. In the first scenario, we consider that there is no unexpected straggler, which means that the computing behaviors of all EC2 instances follow the shift exponential distribution with parameters described in tab:tab008. In the second scenario, we consider that there are some unexpected stragglers. In our experiments, unexpected stragglers will be randomly chosen and each straggler is emulated by delaying the return of computing results such that the computing time observed by the master node is three times of the actual computing time.
new_text: This section evaluates the performance of various distributed computing schemes on a heterogeneous Amazon EC2 cluster. To provide a comprehensive analysis, we designed two experimental scenarios. The first scenario assumes no unexpected stragglers, meaning all EC2 instances operate predictably according to a pre-defined shift exponential distribution. This distribution, characterized by the parameters detailed in Tab. tab008, models typical instance behavior without deviations. This baseline scenario allows us to assess system performance under idealized, consistent conditions. In contrast, the second scenario introduces unexpected stragglers to simulate real-world variability. Here, a subset of instances is randomly selected to act as stragglers by artificially inflating their observed computing times. Specifically, the return of results from these stragglers is delayed so that the master node perceives their completion time as three times the actual time required. This method mimics the unpredictable slowdowns often encountered in distributed systems, enabling us to study how different schemes handle such disruptions. By comparing results from both scenarios, we can isolate the impact of straggler effects on overall system performance.

In high-performance computing, one use for containers is to run
workflows on shared local hardware where teams manage their own
high-performance servers. This can follow one of several design
patterns: users may deploy containers to hardware as a work environment
for a specific project, conatiners may provide per-user persistent
environments, or a single container can act as a common multi-user
environment for a server. In all cases, though, the containerized
approach provides several advantages: First, users may use the same
image and thus work environment on desktop and laptop computers, as
well. The former models provide modularity, while the latter approach is
most similar to a simple shared server. Second, software updates can be
achieved by updating and redeploying the container, rather than tracking
local installs on each server. Third, the containerized environment can
be quickly deployed to other hardware, cloud or local, if more resources
are neccessary or in case of server destruction or failure. In any of
these cases, users need a method to interact with the containers, be it
and IDE, or command-like access and tools such as SSH, which is usually
not part of standard container recipes and must be added. The
Rocker Project provides containers pre-installed with the RStudio IDE.
In cases where users store nontrivial amounts of data for their
projects, data needs to persist beyond the life of the container. This
may be via in shared disks, attached network volumes, or in separate
storage where it is uploaded between sessions. In the case of shared
disks or network-attached volumes, care must be taken to persist user
permissions, and of course backups are still neccessary. When working
with multiple servers, an automation framework such as
Ansible [URL] may be useful for managing
users, permisions, and disks along with containers.
new_text: In high-performance computing, containers are employed to execute workflows on shared on-premises infrastructure where teams maintain dedicated high-performance servers. Common deployment strategies include configuring containers as isolated workspaces for specific projects, persistent per-user environments, or centralized multi-user platforms. The containerization approach offers multiple benefits: users can maintain consistent environments across desktops, laptops, and servers, with the first two models emphasizing modularity and the third resembling traditional shared-server configurations. Updates are streamlined through redeploying modified containers instead of manually updating individual server installations. Additionally, containers enable rapid relocation to alternative hardware—local or cloud-based—when scaling resources or recovering from hardware failure. Interaction with containers typically requires external tools like IDEs or SSH, which are not inherently included in standard container configurations and must be added manually. The Rocker Project addresses this by providing RStudio-integrated containers. For projects involving substantial data, storage solutions such as shared disks, network-attached volumes, or offsite repositories ensure data persistence beyond the container lifecycle. These methods require careful management of user permissions and regular backups. When managing multi-server environments, automation frameworks like Ansible [URL] can synchronize user access, permissions, and storage configurations alongside container deployments.

old_text: In this study, we suggest two language-agnostic authorship attribution models. Both models work with path-based representations of code <cit.>. The first model, called PbRF (Path-based Random Forest), is a random forest trained on term frequencies of tokens and paths in abstract syntax trees (AST). This random forest model matches or improves the state of the art in Java, C++, and Python datasets, even with few available samples per author. The second model, named PbNN (Path-based Neural Network), is an adopted version of code2vec neural network <cit.>. PbNN outperforms PbRF when the number of available samples per author is large. Both models improve state-of-the-art results for Java on a dataset by Yang et al. <cit.>, with 97% and 98% accuracy respectively.

Several recent lines of research have demonstrated a clear benefit in terms of achieving higher accuracy and better generalisation of neural networks trained with corrupted, noisy and synthetically augmented data <cit.>. Training with data augmentation also alleviates the problem of learning from a limited amount of manually annotated data. Similar to the idea presented in 'Snorkel' <cit.>, we designed a number of labelling functions (LF) by compiling a list of rules and keyword patterns for all seven named-entity categories. Additionally, we exploited a 'sense2vec' approach <cit.> which was fine-tuned on the entire MIMIC-III corpora to bootstrap keywords and patterns. 'Sense2vec' is a more complex version of the 'Word2vec' method <cit.> for representation of words as vectors. The major improvement over 'word2vec' is that 'sense2vec' also learns from linguistic annotations of words for sense disambiguation in their embeddings.
new_text: Several recent studies have shown that training neural networks with corrupted, noisy, and synthetically augmented data significantly improves accuracy and generalisation <cit.>. This approach addresses the challenge of limited manually annotated data—a key limitation in many domains. Inspired by the Snorkel framework <cit.>, we developed a set of labelling functions (LFs) by compiling domain-specific rules and keyword patterns across all seven named-entity categories. Complementing this, we employed a fine-tuned 'sense2vec' model <cit.>, utilising the entire MIMIC-III corpus to bootstrap keyword and pattern discovery. 'Sense2vec' extends the 'word2vec' method <cit.> by incorporating linguistic annotations into word vector representations, enabling sense disambiguation through enhanced contextual embeddings.

In general, p(𝐰_i; θ) and q(𝐰_i; λ_i) can be modelled using two general types of probabilistic models: prescribed and implicit <cit.>. For example, ABML <cit.> is a prescribed approach where both distributions are assumed to be diagonal Gaussians. new_text: In probabilistic statistics, the shared prior distribution of model parameters, p(𝐰_i; θ), encapsulates the modeling assumption, while the variational posterior distribution for task-specific parameters, q(𝐰_i; λ_i), serves as an adjustable function designed to balance performance and model complexity effectively. These distributions are typically modeled using two broad categories of probabilistic frameworks: prescribed and implicit <cit.>. For instance, ABML <cit.> utilizes a prescribed method by assuming both distributions adopt diagonal Gaussian forms. This study, however, adopts the implicit modeling framework to flexibly characterize both p(𝐰_i; θ) and q(𝐰_i; λ_i).

old_text: Recent advances in meta-learning have produced state-of-the-art results in many benchmarks of few-shot learning data sets <cit.>. Learning from a few training examples is often difficult and easily leads to over-fitting, especially when no model uncertainty is taken into account. This issue has been addressed by several recent probabilistic meta-learning approaches that incorporate model uncertainty into prediction, notably LLAMA that is based on Laplace method <cit.>, or PLATIPUS <cit.>, Amortised Bayesian Meta-learner (ABML) <cit.> and VERSA <cit.> that use variational inference (VI). However, these works have not thoroughly investigated the generalisation errors for unseen tasks and unseen samples, resulting in limited theoretical generalisation guarantees. Moreover, most of these papers are based on variational functions that may not represent well the richness of the underlying distributions. For instance, a common choice for the variational function relies on the diagonal Gaussian distribution, which can potentially worsen the prediction accuracy given its limited representability.
new_text: Recent advances in meta-learning have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across multiple few-shot learning benchmarks <cit.>. In few-shot scenarios, where models must generalize from extremely limited training examples, overfitting becomes a significant risk—particularly when the learning process ignores model uncertainty. This challenge motivates the development of probabilistic meta-learning frameworks, which explicitly incorporate uncertainty into predictions. Several notable approaches have emerged in this space, each adopting distinct statistical methodologies to approximate uncertainty. For instance, LLAMA employs the Laplace approximation to estimate posterior distributions <cit.>, while PLATIPUS <cit.>, the Amortised Bayesian Meta-learner (ABML) <cit.>, and VERSA <cit.> utilize variational inference (VI) to approximate complex probability distributions. Despite these innovations, a critical limitation remains: most of these methods have not rigorously analyzed generalization errors for novel tasks or new data samples. This gap results in weak theoretical guarantees for their performance in real-world applications. Furthermore, the choice of variational approximations—which are central to methods like VI—can constrain model performance. Many studies rely on simplified variational distributions, such as diagonal Gaussian forms, to reduce computational complexity. However, diagonal Gaussians ignore correlations between variables by assuming independence, which limits their ability to capture the full complexity of the underlying data distribution. This restriction may degrade prediction accuracy, particularly in cases where inter-variable dependencies are essential for reliable inference.

old_text: Learning emulators at large-scale This task is closely related to the grand AI challenge of common-sense learning. In humans, common-sense is hard-coded through rich experience <cit.>; it is reasonable to expect that approximating human emulators will require extensive hard-coding as well. In rendering this task tractable, We join <cit.> in advocating a tighter loop between learning and programming to represent knowledge: AI should be extensively utilized in hard-coding its own common-sense. Whereas earlier approaches typically consisted of non-executable, relational knowledge graphs (KGs) <cit.>, in our case knowledge can be represented by code, executable in interactive simulations. KGs will likely be useful for populating an initial “seed emulator”, as will AKBC methods for learning object <cit.> and action <cit.> properties at scale. In <cit.>, multimodal simulations are used to evaluate automatic affordance extraction. In <cit.>, game designers (for human games) utilized NLU methods for learning object affordance semantics. Finally, as symbolic knowledge is by nature incomplete, it will likely need to be superseded by geometric knowledge representations <cit.>.

Crowd motion flows can be very instrumental in describing group behavior in humans. Several literatures have explained crowd motion behavior on basis of physics and biological-inspired models <cit.>. However, majority of such works primarily focus on physics-inspired models for crowd behavior analysis. These methods claim that the physics-based models can capture most of the dynamics of crowd motions. In physics-inspired models, the dominant flow in the crowd can be considered analogous to fluid. In an another approach, sparse human crowd can be considered similar to motion of gases <cit.>. Therefore, it is believed that the theory of fluid dynamics, statistical thermodynamics, concept of Brownian motion and many other physical concepts can only be employed after certain relaxations in the root models. In <cit.>, Hughes pointed out the similarities between physics and the actual crowd. He described the crowd as a component of fluids from the physic's perspective. However, the concept is complex as interactions between individuals is far complicated than fluid particle interactions. Similarly, Vicsek et al. <cit.> have developed force-based models to describe collective motion in crowd. The collective motion is described in terms of velocity, orientation, correlation function and fluid dynamics. Helbing et al. <cit.> have developed a physical model that uses density and pressure quantities to mark turbulent flows and stop-and-go phenomena in crowd. In <cit.>, the authors categorized crowd models as microscopic, mesoscopic and macroscopic. The macroscopic model considers crowd as a single unit comprising of all individuals. In the microscopic model, a person is considered as a fundamental unit of the crowd. The mesoscopic model is a combination of both macroscopic and microscopic model. However, the difference between the former two models is not crisp. In <cit.>, Johansson et al. have discussed about different dynamics of crowd that lead to various crowd safety issues.
The authors in <cit.> have used simple set of rules of interactions between neighboring particles in order to explain collective behavior with a special focus on group intelligence in human crowd. In <cit.>, the authors have proposed a Particle Swarm Optimization model (PSO) to simulate crowd. The authors in <cit.> presented a physical modeling framework that describes the intelligent, non-local, and anisotropic behavior of pedestrians. In <cit.>, the Lagrangian (moving) coordinate system has been used for simulation and modeling of crowd flows. The authors in <cit.> have developed a multi-class continuum modeling based on social force model to simulate bilinear crowd flows. The authors in <cit.> have developed a dynamic variant of Vicsek model to study collective motion in panicked human crowds.
new_text:
Crowd motion flows are essential for understanding group behavior in human collectives. Numerous studies have explored crowd dynamics using physics- and biology-inspired models <cit.>. While most research focuses on physics-based frameworks for analyzing crowd behavior, these approaches argue that physical principles can capture the essential dynamics of crowd motion. In physics-inspired models, the dominant flow is often likened to fluid behavior, whereas sparse crowds can analogously be compared to gaseous motion <cit.>. Consequently, concepts such as fluid dynamics, statistical thermodynamics, and Brownian motion are typically applied only after relaxing idealized assumptions in foundational models. Hughes <cit.> highlighted parallels between crowd dynamics and physical systems, conceptualizing crowds as fluid components from a physics perspective. However, he noted that individual interactions in crowds are far more complex than interactions between fluid particles. Vicsek et al. <cit.> introduced force-based models to describe collective crowd motion in terms of velocity, orientation, correlation functions, and fluid dynamics. Helbing et al. <cit.> developed a physical model incorporating density and pressure to characterize turbulent flows and stop-and-go patterns in crowds. In <cit.>, the authors classify crowd models into three categories: microscopic, mesoscopic, and macroscopic. The macroscopic approach treats the crowd as a single cohesive unit, while the microscopic model defines individuals as fundamental units. The mesoscopic model bridges these two perspectives, though the distinction between the macroscopic and microscopic frameworks remains blurred. Johansson et al. <cit.> analyzed diverse crowd dynamics that contribute to safety risks, emphasizing the need for robust modeling techniques. 

Researchers have employed simplified rules for inter-particle interactions to explain collective behavior and group intelligence in crowds <cit.>. A Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) model has been proposed to simulate crowd dynamics <cit.>. Another study presents a physical modeling framework capturing pedestrians’ intelligent, non-local, and anisotropic behaviors <cit.>. The Lagrangian coordinate system has also been utilized for modeling crowd flows <cit.>. A multi-class continuum model based on the social force framework was developed to simulate bilinear crowd flows <cit.>, and a dynamic variant of the Vicsek model has been applied to study collective motion in panicked human crowds <cit.>.

All these types of undirected motions are considered as passive motion. This is because Brownian particle does not participate actively in this motion. On the other hand, active [The term "active" implies that the individuals particles or units move acquiring energy from the environment.] motion of Brownian particles depend on the supply of energy. In biological systems, this kind of active self-driven Brownian motion can be observed at different scales, ranging from cells <cit.> or simple micro-organisms to higher scale organisms like bird or fish. Finally human crowd movement can be demonstrated as active Brownian motion. Such type of motions can be applied to confined systems of particles (like human traffic flow in two dimension) that performs collective motion under far from equilibrium conditions. Now, one major question arises. How the known picture of passive motion mentioned in (<ref>) needs to be modified to incorporate self or internal "activity" of the particles? Here, the main assumption is, there is additional inflow of energy that causes active motion and can be represented practically by negative dissipation in the direction of motion. Thus, it can be modeled by negative friction β(r,v), i.e., represented as a function of position and velocity. Usually this kind of systems are far from equilibrium. The negative friction force does not obey fluctuation-dissipation relationship implying the system is considered as homogeneous in space implying β(r,v) = β(v). This is considered as a frictional force applied to the component of the motion in the direction of the particle connecting vectors that helps particle moving together in the same direction. Thus, (<ref>) is modified below and is represented as given in (<ref>),
new_text: The equation described in (<ref>) characterizes a passive Brownian system expected to reach equilibrium over extended timescales, as opposing forces balance to produce a unique stationary state governed by the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. All unidirectional motions within this framework are classified as "passive" because the Brownian particles do not actively contribute to their movement. In contrast, active [where "active" denotes that individual particles or units derive energy from external sources to sustain motion] Brownian motion relies on external energy input. In biological contexts, such active self-driven motion emerges across multiple scales, from single cells <cit.> or microorganisms to larger entities like birds and fish. Human crowd dynamics also exemplify active Brownian motion, applicable to confined systems (e.g., two-dimensional traffic flow) exhibiting collective motion far from equilibrium. A critical question arises: how must the passive motion framework in (<ref>) be revised to account for the intrinsic "activity" of particles? The central assumption involves an external energy input enabling active motion, represented through effective negative dissipation along the direction of motion. This can be modeled via a position- and velocity-dependent negative friction coefficient β(r,v). Typically, such systems remain far from equilibrium, as the negative friction force violates the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Under spatial homogeneity, β(r,v) simplifies to β(v), representing a frictional force acting along the particle-connection vector component to align motion direction. Consequently, (<ref>) is modified as expressed in (<ref>), incorporating these active dynamics.

Background models are utilized to segment the foreground in videos, generally regarded as object of interest towards further video processing. Therefore, providing a robust background model in various computer vision applications is an essential preliminary task. However, modeling the background in complex real-world scenarios is still challenging due to presence of dynamic backgrounds, jitter induced by unstable camera, occlusion, illumination changes. None of the approaches proposed so far could address all the challenges in their model. Moreover, current background models models are mostly scene-specific. Therefore, DNN models need to be retrained adjusting their weights for each particular scene and non-DNN models require parameter tuning for optimal result on different video sequences, which makes them unable to extend to unseen scenes.

new_text: Background models are essential for foreground segmentation in videos, typically identifying the object of interest for subsequent video processing tasks. Consequently, developing a robust background model is a critical prerequisite for numerous computer vision applications. However, modeling the background in complex real-world scenarios remains challenging due to dynamic backgrounds, camera instability-induced jitter, occlusions, and illumination variations. Existing approaches have yet to comprehensively address these challenges within a single model. Furthermore, current background models are predominantly scene-specific: DNN-based models require retraining and weight adjustments for each scene, while non-DNN models necessitate parameter tuning to achieve optimal performance on different video sequences, limiting their generalizability to unseen scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a generative low-dimensional background model (G-LBM) estimation approach that is universally applicable across diverse video sequences. old_text: In situations where an imprecise or inaccurate annotation of the data is much cheaper to obtain compared to an accurate annotation, weakly-supervised learning can be taken into consideration. <cit.> argue that a large number of noisy annotations should convey enough information about the task to be performed with reasonable accuracy while reducing the burden on the data annotator. The aim is thus to replace time-consuming annotation procedures, yielding the way for potentially labeling larger datasets. <cit.> have shown it is possible to successfully learn a segmentation task in the medical domain by using axis-aligned bounding boxes, derived from 6 points. Instead of full, pixel-wise segmentation labels, less time consuming labelling techniques include bounding boxes <cit.>, scribbles <cit.>, or points <cit.>.
new_text: Weakly-supervised learning becomes a viable approach when obtaining precise, high-quality data annotations is significantly more resource-intensive than gathering imprecise or error-prone labels. The core argument, as proposed by <cit.>, is that even a large volume of noisy annotations can retain sufficient task-relevant information to enable models to achieve reasonable accuracy, while substantially alleviating the annotation effort required of human experts. This strategy prioritizes scalability over annotation perfection, aiming to supplant laborious labeling workflows with faster, albeit noisier, alternatives. For instance, in the medical domain, <cit.> demonstrated that axis-aligned bounding boxes—generated from as few as six annotated points—can effectively train a segmentation model, outperforming the need for meticulous pixel-wise labeling. Similarly, <cit.> highlight that techniques like basic bounding boxes, freeform scribbles <cit.>, and sparse point annotations <cit.> offer practical compromises: they reduce the time and expertise needed for annotation while maintaining a balance between label sufficiency and computational feasibility. These methods collectively shift the focus from error-free labels to cost-effective data acquisition, enabling the creation of larger training datasets without incurring prohibitive annotation overhead.

Even if almost all the mobile applications are distributed by authorized stores (e.g., Google Play store for Android), they can still be harmful. new_text: When a user subscribes to paid services, she is typically able to identify unauthorized access due to immediate financial or account-related consequences. However, in cases involving data extraction—such as the unauthorized collection of personal information like names, addresses, or call logs—the user remains unaware of the breach. This is because such attacks often operate covertly, lacking visible signs of exploitation. Although most mobile applications are distributed through authorized platforms like the Google Play Store for Android, these marketplaces are not foolproof. Even apps from legitimate stores can contain malicious functionalities. Security checks, conducted both automatically by systems and manually by reviewers, often fail to detect these threats. The reason lies in the nature of the attack: since it relies solely on standard HTTP requests—commonly used for data transfer rather than malicious activity—the behavior does not resemble traditional malware or phishing attempts. Consequently, apps available on both iOS and Android stores could potentially execute such data extractions without triggering alerts. In practical terms, depending on the user’s mobile service provider, these applications might access and extract sensitive user information without the user’s knowledge or the system’s detection, highlighting a significant gap in current mobile security frameworks.

Real-time semantic video segmentation is a challenging task due to the strict requirements of inference speed.
Recent approaches mainly devote great efforts to reducing the model size for high efficiency.
In this paper, we rethink this problem from a different viewpoint: using knowledge contained in compressed videos. We propose a simple and effective framework, dubbed TapLab, to tap into resources from the compressed domain.
Specifically, we design a fast feature warping module using motion vectors for acceleration. To reduce the noise introduced by motion vectors, we design a residual-guided correction module and a residual-guided frame selection module using residuals.
new_text: Real-time semantic video segmentation is a challenging task due to the strict requirements for inference speed. Recent approaches mainly focus on reducing model size for higher efficiency. In this paper, we rethink this problem from a different perspective: leveraging knowledge contained in compressed videos. We propose a simple and effective framework, dubbed TapLab, to tap into the compressed domain's resources. Specifically, we design a fast feature warping module using motion vectors to accelerate inference. To reduce the noise introduced by motion vectors, we design residual-guided correction and frame selection modules that utilize residuals.

As shown in Table <ref>, when resolution of the input region is low enough, the inference speed grows disproportionately to the shrinking rate of the input shape, which means the dominator of inference time changes from computational costs to I/O and communication operations (e.g., the time for `feed_dict' in Tensorflow).
new_text: Given the crucial role of residual maps in video codecs for motion compensation, we introduce the residual-guided correction (RGC) module to enhance the quality of propagated features. The correction process is illustrated in Fig. . This method increases accuracy from 64.4% to 68.2% (BL2), as detailed in Table <ref>. To address boundary-cropping issues, the "stride" parameter is adjusted to maintain overlapping regions. When the stride value is smaller than the region’s side length (e.g., 256 versus 512), the candidate regions overlap rather than align adjacently, ensuring that high-response objects cut by region boundaries remain predominantly within the overlapping area. The RGC module operates in parallel with FFW, maintaining computational efficiency without additional runtime. As demonstrated in Table <ref>, when input resolution is sufficiently low, inference speed increases disproportionately relative to the reduction in input size, indicating that the dominant bottleneck shifts from computational costs to I/O and communication operations (e.g., `feed_dict` in Tensorflow).

old_text: **Sample Extraction.** Training data consist of 32 × 32 samples extracted from 100 binary documents (forms, emails, memos, etc.) scanned at 300 dpi of the IIT-CDIP Test Collection 1.0 <cit.>. For sampling, the pages are split longitudinally into 30 virtual shreds (amount estimated for the usual A4 paper shredders). Next, the shreds are individually thresholded with Sauvola's algorithm <cit.> to cope with small fluctuations in pixel values of the original images. Sample pairs are extracted page-wise, which means that the samples in a pair come from the same document. The extraction process starts with adjacent shreds in order to collect positive sample pairs (limited to 1,000 pairs per document). Negative pairs are collected subsequently, but limited to the number of positive pairs. During extraction, the shreds are scanned from top to bottom, cropping samples every two pixels. Pairs with more than 80% blank pixels are considered ambiguous, and then they are discarded for future training. Finally, the damage caused by mechanical shredding is roughly simulated with the application of salt-and-pepper random noise on the two rightmost pixels of the r-samples, and on the two leftmost pixels of the l-samples.
new_text: **Sample Extraction.** The training data comprise 32 × 32 samples extracted from 100 binary documents (forms, emails, memos, etc.) scanned at 300 dpi from the IIT-CDIP Test Collection 1.0 <cit.>. To facilitate sampling, each page is divided longitudinally into 30 virtual shreds (a number estimated to reflect standard A4 paper shredders). These shreds are individually thresholded using Sauvola’s algorithm <cit.> to mitigate minor variations in pixel values of the original images. Sample pairs are extracted page-wise, ensuring the samples in each pair originate from the same document. The extraction prioritizes adjacent shreds to collect positive pairs, limited to 1,000 pairs per document. Negative pairs are then collected, with a maximum count equal to the number of positive pairs. Throughout, shreds are scanned from top to bottom, with samples cropped every two pixels. Pairs containing more than 80% blank pixels are classified as ambiguous and subsequently discarded. Finally, damage caused by mechanical shredding is roughly simulated by applying salt-and-pepper random noise: on the two rightmost pixels of r-samples and the two leftmost pixels of l-samples.

When the framerate is high, motion between frames is small, and a zero offset is often a reasonable starting point for association.

new_text: Figure <ref> depicts the detailed structure of a transformer encoder block. The core component within a Transformer Encoder block is the Multi-Head Attention layer, which employs the self-attention mechanism <cit.>. A defining feature of the self-attention model is its invariance to input ordering; that is, it produces identical outputs regardless of the permutation of N input representations. This characteristic is problematic in scenarios where sequential processing of novel images in a specific order is required. To address this limitation, positional encoding P is introduced to the input representation r. The combined input (r + P) is then projected into distinct query (Q), key (K), and value (V) representations. Research in <cit.> indicates that duplicating the self-attention mechanism into H separate heads allows each head to focus on different aspects of the input by utilizing unique sets of query (Q_h), key (K_h), and value (V_h) representations. The outputs from these heads are concatenated and subsequently linearly transformed to match the original dimensionality of r using a weight matrix W_out and a bias vector b_out. We control the relative location of representations in a particular latent subspace, based on the similarity of their respective data points according to the corresponding criterion. new_text: We propose a polarized-VAE to disentangle the latent space into subspaces corresponding to distinct factors of variation. new_text: By Marcus-Tardos theorem, the number of corners cannot grow beyond a certain threshold, otherwise the matrix would fail to be simple. This property allows us to eventually identify two rows or two columns with sufficiently small Hamming distance, resulting in contractible pairs. However, maintaining the matrix's simplicity throughout the contraction process introduces certain technical challenges. To address this, we employ a two-step algorithm: In the first step, we construct a sequence of partition coarsenings over the matrix, and in the second step, we extract the actual contraction sequence. The overall algorithm, which takes A (or σ) as input and outputs the contraction sequence, operates in polynomial time relative to *n*. It can be implemented in quadratic time, or potentially even faster, if provided with a list of pointers to A's corners rather than the raw matrix itself.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is known as one of the major causes of dementia and is characterized by slow progression over several years, with no treatments or available medicines. In this regard, there have been efforts to identify the risk of developing AD in its earliest time. While many of the previous works considered cross-sectional analysis, more recent studies have focused on the diagnosis and prognosis of AD with longitudinal or time series data in a way of disease progression modeling (DPM). Under the same problem settings, in this work, we propose a novel computational framework that forecasts the phenotypic measurements of MRI biomarkers and predicts the clinical statuses at multiple future time points.
However, in handling time series data, it generally faces with many unexpected missing observations. In regard to such an unfavorable situation, we define a secondary problem of estimating those missing values and tackle it in a systematic way by taking account of temporal and multivariate relations inherent in time series data. Concretely, we propose a deep recurrent network that jointly tackles the three problems of (i) missing value imputation, (ii) phenotypic measurements forecasting, and (iii) clinical status prediction of a subject based on his/her longitudinal imaging biomarkers. Notably, the learnable model parameters of our network are trained in an end-to-end manner with our circumspectly defined loss function. In our experiments over The Alzheimer’s Disease Prediction Of Longitudinal Evolution (TADPOLE) challenge cohort, we measured performance for various metrics and compared our method to competing methods in the literature. Exhaustive analyses and ablation studies were also conducted to better confirm the effectiveness of our method.
new_text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is one of the leading causes of dementia and is marked by a slow, progressive decline in cognitive function over years. Due to its insidious onset and lack of effective treatments or medications to halt progression, identifying AD risk at the earliest possible stage has become a critical research focus. Historically, many studies relied on cross-sectional analyses, which examine a single point in time and limit the ability to capture dynamic changes. However, recent advances have shifted toward longitudinal or time series approaches, as these align more closely with the goal of disease progression modeling (DPM). By tracking changes over time, researchers aim to better understand and predict how AD evolves in individuals. Within this context, we introduce a novel computational framework designed to forecast phenotypic measurements derived from MRI biomarkers and predict clinical status at multiple future time points.  

A significant challenge in working with longitudinal data lies in the frequent occurrence of missing observations, which can arise from various factors such as participant dropout or imaging limitations. To address this issue systematically, we formulate a secondary task focused on estimating these missing values. Our approach leverages both temporal patterns and multivariate relationships inherent in the data. Specifically, we develop a deep recurrent network capable of simultaneously tackling three interrelated problems: (i) imputing missing values in the time series, (ii) forecasting future phenotypic measurements, and (iii) predicting a subject’s clinical status based on their longitudinal imaging biomarkers. The model is trained in an end-to-end fashion, with learnable parameters optimized using a loss function carefully designed to balance these objectives.  

We evaluated our method using the Alzheimer’s Disease Prediction Of Longitudinal Evolution (TADPOLE) challenge dataset, a benchmark cohort for AD progression studies. Our performance was assessed using multiple metrics and benchmarked against existing methods in the literature to highlight its advantages. Furthermore, we conducted exhaustive analyses and ablation studies to validate the contribution of individual components of our framework, ensuring that the observed improvements stem from the integrated design of the model. These experiments provide robust evidence of the framework’s effectiveness in handling the complexities of longitudinal AD data.

In this regard, we devised a novel analysis method of the cell states in our LSTM. To determine which cell states contributed to the identification of the clinical statuses, we estimated the correlation between a patient's disease statuses over time and the corresponding cell state representations. Specifically, we first collected the internal cell representations of ≈ 19 subjects (19.2±5.0)[This value represented the mean and standard deviation over the number of subjects in 5-fold cross-validation.], who experienced status-conversion during our period of interest, and then measured the correlations between the change of the values in the cell states and a transition of the patient's disease status (0: no conversion and 1: conversion) with point-biserial correlation coefficients.

new_text: Despite achieving superior results in MRI biomarker forecasting and clinical status prediction with our deep recurrent network, understanding the internal state dynamics of our model is critical. To address this, we developed a novel method to analyze the cell states within our LSTM. Specifically, we investigated which cell states were associated with identifying clinical status changes by estimating correlations between disease status progression in patients over time and their corresponding cell state representations. We first extracted internal cell representations from ≈19 subjects (19.2±5.0)[This value represented the mean and standard deviation over the number of subjects in 5-fold cross-validation.] who exhibited status conversions during the observation period, then computed point-biserial correlation coefficients between the cell state value changes and the patient’s binary disease status (0: no conversion, 1: conversion). Subjects were categorized by disease transitions as follows: (i) ≈3 subjects (3.6±2.3) transitioning from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), (ii) ≈13 subjects (13.4±6.0) transitioning from MCI to Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and (iii) ≈2 subjects (2.0±1.6) progressing through CN, MCI, and AD [CN-MCI-AD]. These steps are described in more detail in the subsections that follow.

old_text: This paper builds on recent developments in BN structure learning under causal insufficiency with a novel structure learning algorithm, called CCHM, that combines constraint-based and score-based learning with causal effects to learn GBNs. The constraint-based part of CCHM adopts features from the state-of-the-art cFCI algorithm, whereas the score-based part is based on traditional hill-climbing greedy search that minimises the BIC score. CCHM applies Pearl's do-calculus as a method to orientate the edges that both constraint-based and score-based learning fail to do so from observational data. The results show that CCHM outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithms in the majority of the experiments, which include both randomised and real-world GBNs.

new_text: A problem with K variables and M constraints (M ≥ K) is termed reverse convex programming (RCP) if the objective function u and constraints f_i (i = 1, 2, ..., M) are quasi-convex. Equality constraints of the form ∑_{k=1}^K w_k y_k = c (c ∈ ℝ, w_k ∈ ℝ) can be expressed as two linear (and reverse convex) inequalities: ∑_{k=1}^K w_k y_k ≤ c and ∑_{k=1}^K w_k y_k ≥ c. Due to the non-convex feasible region, global optimization for RCP is challenging; numerous algorithms to achieve this have been proposed in the literature (see, e.g., <cit.>). For analysis, define the feasible region of (<ref>) as 𝒜 := {y : f_i(y) ≥ 0 for all i ∈ {1, 2, ..., M}} and let ℐ(y) := {i ∈ {1, 2, ..., M} : f_i(y) = 0} for y ∈ 𝒜.

Achieving high performance with DL-based methods and models, often requires sufficient labeled data which can be difficult and costly to obtain, especially for audio signals <cit.>.
As a way to lift the restrictions imposed by the limited amount of audio data, different published works employ transfer learning on tasks were only small datasets are available <cit.>.

In this approach, an embedding model is initially trained on a supervised task characterized by large-scale data availability. Subsequently, this pretrained model functions as a feature extractor, generating input representations that are leveraged to train another model on a distinct task suffering from limited data availability <cit.>.

Another challenge facing physics-based methods is synthesizing multi-modal long-term human motions. Previous work has elicited long-term human motions with hierarchical RL <cit.> or user interactive control <cit.>. However, these approaches still need to define high-level tasks of the agent or require human interaction. We argue that removing these requirements could be critical for applications like automated motion generation and large-scale character animation. Thus, we take a different approach to long-term human motion synthesis by leveraging the temporal dependence of human motion. In particular, we propose a dual-policy control framework where a kinematic policy learns to predict multi-modal future motions based on the past motion and a latent variable used to model human intent, while an RFC-based control policy learns to imitate the output motions of the kinematic policy to produce physically-plausible motions. Experiments on a large-scale human motion dataset, Human3.6M <cit.>, show that our approach with RFC and dual policy control can synthesize stable long-term human motions without any task guidance or user input.

**The role of NOSC.**
In this present work, NOSC as the auditory feature code is randomly generated under the constraints imposed by NOSC requirements. The connection from the AF layer, which takes NOSC as input, to the AVI layer is fixed and does not have any plasticity during continual learning in our experiments. The inspiration for such structural design came from the following experimental phenomenon: 1. The brain has better self-learning ability for hearing; 2. The hearing has a significant impact on vision; 3. The development of hearing is earlier than vision. Although this design is reasonable to some extent, it is more biological plausible that different perceptions do interact with each other during the learning process. One of the future work is to study how to integrate multi-modal signals in the case of both visual and auditory plasticity.
new_text: **The role of NOSC.** In this work, NOSC, used as the auditory feature code, is randomly generated under the constraints imposed by NOSC requirements. The connection from the AF layer (which takes NOSC as input) to the AVI layer is fixed and remains without plasticity during continual learning in our experiments. The structural design was inspired by the following experimental observations: (1) the brain exhibits enhanced self-learning capacity for hearing; (2) hearing significantly influences vision; and (3) auditory development precedes visual development. Although this design is reasonably plausible, it is even more biologically plausible that different perceptual modalities interact during learning. One future direction is to investigate how to integrate multimodal signals when both visual and auditory plasticity are present.

old_text: In the late 1980s, researchers discovered the sequential learning problem known as catastrophic forgetting in the connectionist networks <cit.>. With the great success of deep learning in the fields of perceptual recognition <cit.> and board games <cit.>, researchers once again started to pay attention to the problem of catastrophic forgetting, as the existing AI technology facing with the difficulty of continuous learning in the continuously changing environment <cit.>. Within the framework of artificial neural network (ANN) with backpropagation (BP) algorithm <cit.>, researchers have defined a series of continual learning tasks <cit.>, such as incremental learning of new instances, new classes, and the mixture of new instances and classes, and have proposed many constructive solutions to these specific tasks. The mainstream methods proposed can be divided into the following topics: regularizations of the network <cit.>, parameters isolation <cit.>, dynamic structure <cit.> , memory-based consolidation <cit.>, network with attention mechanism <cit.>, and the dual system inspired by complementary learning system theory in the brain <cit.>. Although the blossom of new methods, they are still far from the level of human continual learning. How to achieve human-level of continual lifelong learning still needs more exploration and research.
new_text: In the late 1980s, researchers discovered a sequential learning problem known as catastrophic forgetting in connectionist networks <cit.>. With the remarkable success of deep learning in the domains of perceptual recognition <cit.> and board games <cit.>, researchers once again began paying attention to the problem of catastrophic forgetting, as existing AI technologies faced the difficulty of continuous learning in continuously changing environments <cit.>. Within the framework of artificial neural networks (ANNs) with backpropagation (BP) algorithms <cit.>, researchers have defined various continual learning tasks <cit.>, such as incremental learning of new instances, new classes, and mixing new instances and classes, and have proposed numerous constructive solutions to these specific tasks. The mainstream methods proposed can be categorized into the following topics: network regularizations <cit.>, parameter isolation <cit.>, dynamic network structures <cit.>, memory-based consolidation <cit.>, networks with attention mechanisms <cit.>, and dual systems inspired by complementary learning system theory in the brain <cit.>. Although a proliferation of new methods exists, they remain far from the level of human continual learning. Achieving human-level continual lifelong learning remains an open challenge requiring further exploration and research.

**MNIST10-FV.**  
To create the MNIST10-FV dataset, we designed an MNIST10-CNN and trained it using the MNIST10-(TR50-TE50) dataset. The network structure of the MNIST10-CNN is similar to that of LeNet-5, and the dimension of the V-FV in this network is 15. During training, we recorded the highest validation accuracy (92.6%) achievable by the MNIST10-CNN. Using four ranges of quality control parameters—60%–62%, 70%–72%, 80%–82%, and above 90%—we extracted four levels of V-FV from the MNIST10-(TR50-TE50) dataset, labeled MNIST10-FV1 through MNIST10-FV4. We visualized the distribution of these four V-FV levels using t-SNE (see Figure <ref>). The impact of quality control is evident: higher quality leads to better separability.

In the research context, the adapter plugging strategy <cit.> is usually fixed, dense, and handcrafted. Consequently, it is less flexible and discriminative with a higher computational cost in many complicated situations. Moreover, the adapter module structure is also predefined and fixed for different domains, leading to the weakness in cross-domain adaptation. Therefore, how to automatically set up the adapter plugging strategy
and adaptively fulfill the adapter structure design are crucial for effective multi-domain learning.
Motivated by this observation, we propose a novel NAS-driven scheme for multi-domain learning based on Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Specifically,
we accomplish the task of automatically finding the effective adapter plugging strategy by NAS, and meanwhile make full use of NAS to search the adapter structures adaptively. In this way, our scheme has the following advantages: 1) more flexible and sparser adapter plugging with better efficiency and generalization by NAS; and 2) more discriminative adapter modules with better adaptation to different domains. As a result, the multi-domain model we obtain is often more compact, discriminative, and domain adaptive with a relatively low computational cost.
new_text: In the research setting, the adapter plugging strategy <cit.> is typically fixed, densely connected, and manually designed. Consequently, it is less flexible and discriminative, incurring higher computational costs in complex scenarios. Moreover, the adapter module structure is predefined and static across different domains, contributing to poor performance in cross-domain adaptation. Therefore, automatically determining the adapter plugging strategy and adaptively designing the adapter architecture are crucial for effective multi-domain learning. Motivated by this observation, we propose a novel NAS-driven scheme for multi-domain learning. Specifically, we automatically identify effective adapter plugging strategies using NAS and leverage NAS to search for adaptive adapter architectures. In this way, our scheme offers the following advantages: 1) more flexible and sparse adapter configurations with enhanced efficiency and generalization; and 2) more discriminative adapter modules that adapt better to different domains. As a result, the resulting multi-domain model is often more compact, discriminative, and domain-adaptive while incurring relatively low computational costs.

Code-mixing is a phenomenon which arises mainly in multilingual societies. Multilingual people, who are well versed in their native languages and also English speakers, tend to code-mix using English-based phonetic typing and the insertion of anglicisms in their main language. This linguistic phenomenon poses a great challenge to conventional NLP domains such as Sentiment Analysis, Machine Translation, and Text Summarization, to name a few. In this work, we focus on working out a plausible solution to the domain of Code-Mixed Sentiment Analysis. This work was done as participation in the SemEval-2020 Sentimix Task, where we focused on the sentiment analysis of English-Hindi code-mixed sentences. our username for the submission was "sainik.mahata" and team name was "JUNLP". We used feature extraction algorithms in conjunction with traditional machine learning algorithms such as SVR and Grid Search in an attempt to solve the task. Our approach garnered an f1-score of 66.2% when tested using metrics prepared by the organizers of the task.

Addressing code-mixed sentiment analysis, we submitted to the SemEval-2020 Sentimix Task, analyzing English-Hindi code-mixed sentences under the username "sainik.mahata" and team name "JUNLP" (2). Our system combined feature extraction with traditional algorithms (SVR, Grid Search) and achieved a 66.2% f1-score on the task's evaluation metrics (3).

old_text:
We propose a model of the fake news cascade.
Our model assumes that a cascade consists of two cascading processes, namely, the one owing to the original news and the other owing to the correction of the news.
new_text: We present a model for analyzing fake news cascades, which posits that each cascade comprises two cascading processes: one driven by the original news and the other triggered by its correction.

old_text:
In this study, we propose a point process model of the information cascade of fake news posts by extending the Time-Dependent Hawkes process (TiDeH) <cit.>, which is a state-of-the-art model for predicting the popularity dynamics of a cascade.
The proposed model describes the fake news cascade as a two-stage process (Fig. <ref>). Initially, a cascade spreads as an ordinary news item. After a correction time, the second cascade emerges to disclose and rectify the falsity of the original news.
To validate the proposed method, we collected two datasets of cascade of fake news from Twitter.
We demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing methods for accurately predicting the fake news spreading in future. Furthermore, the experimental results suggest that our methodology is useful in inferring the correction time of a fake news based on the time series (i.e., posted or re-shared times).
new_text: We propose a point process model of fake news cascades by extending the Time-Dependent Hawkes process (TiDeH) <cit.>, a state-of-the-art tool for predicting cascade popularity dynamics. The model characterizes fake news as a two-stage process (Fig. <ref>): initially spreading as ordinary news, followed by a secondary cascade that corrects the falsity after a defined correction time. Validation uses two Twitter datasets of fake news cascades, demonstrating superior predictive accuracy compared to existing methods. Experimental results also show utility in inferring correction times using time series data (post/re-share times).

There have been numerous attempts at an automatic detection of fake news and rumors <cit.>.
Typically, fake news is detected based on the textual content of the news.
This problem is formulated as a classification task where multiple categories of features from the sentences <cit.> or the word vectors <cit.> are applied to classification methods.
Interestingly, it has been shown that the temporal aspect of the information cascade, i.e., the posts and re-shares related to the original news, improves the performance of rumor detection <cit.>, fake news detection <cit.>, rumor stance classification <cit.>, and the detection of the fake retweeting account <cit.>.
These works have suggested that an accurate temporal model of such cascades is essential to improve the performance of the fake news detection.
Although several works have developed a temporal model for cascades on meme data <cit.> and Twitter <cit.>, little attention has been paid to the modeling of the fake news cascades.
new_text: Automatic detection of fake news and rumors has been extensively explored <cit.>. Fake news detection is based on textual content of the news, typically framed as a classification task using features extracted from sentences <cit.>, word vectors <cit.>, or similar inputs. Studies show that the temporal aspect of information cascades (posts and re-shares) enhances performance in rumor detection <cit.>, fake news detection <cit.>, rumor stance classification <cit.>, and identification of fake retweeting accounts <cit.>. These findings demonstrate that accurate temporal modeling of cascades is essential to improve fake news detection. While temporal models for cascades have been developed on meme data <cit.> and Twitter <cit.>, modeling of fake news cascades has received little attention.

Data representation learning <cit.> is an important yet challenging task in machine learning community.
Recently, deep neural networks (DNN) have made impressive progress in representation learning for various types of data, including speech, image, and natural language, in which dedicated networks such as RNN <cit.>, CNN <cit.> and Transformer <cit.> are effective at learning compact representations to improve the predictive performance.

new_text: Data representation learning <cit.> remains a critical yet challenging task within the machine learning community. Recently, deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved significant advancements in representation learning across diverse data modalities—including speech, image, and natural language—utilizing architectures like RNNs <cit.>, CNNs <cit.>, and Transformers <cit.> to effectively learn compact representations that enhance predictive performance. However, many real-world applications, such as click-through rate prediction in recommendation systems and online advertising, continue to depend on manual feature engineering to capture interactions within the higher-order feature space, which requires crafting combinatorial features. For instance, a third-order interaction feature such as "Gender ⊗ Age ⊗ Income" can enhance model performance by capturing nuanced patterns related to the types of recommended commodities. Such high-order interactive features introduce non-linear decision boundaries into the lightweight models commonly used in practice while maintaining minimal impact on inference speed. Moreover, these features offer strong interpretability—unlike DNNs—which are often criticized for their black-box nature.

To enable effective CTDE for multi-agent Q-learning, it is essential that the optimal joint action should be equivalent to the collection of individual optimal actions of agents, which is called the IGM (Individual-Global-Max) principle <cit.>. Due to the exponential joint action space, the greedy action selection in the whole joint action space becomes intractable. To address this scalability issue, VDN <cit.> and QMIX <cit.> propose two sufficient conditions of IGM to factorize the joint action-value function. However, these two decomposition methods suffer from structural constraints and severely limit the joint action-value function class they can represent. The result of Wang et al. <cit.> indicates that the incompleteness of joint value function class may lead to poor performance or even unbounded divergence in off-policy training. To address this structural limitation, QTRAN <cit.> proposes a factorization method expressing the complete value function space induced by the IGM consistency, but its exact implementation is known to be computationally intractable and approximate versions have instable and poor performance in complex domains <cit.>. Therefore, achieving effective scalability remains an open problem for cooperative MARL.
new_text: Ensuring effective CTDE in multi-agent Q-learning requires that the optimal joint action corresponds to the union of individual agents’ optimal actions, a property termed the IGM (Individual-Global-Max) principle. However, the exponential growth of the joint action space renders greedy selection over the entire joint action space computationally infeasible. To mitigate this scalability challenge, VDN and QMIX introduce two sufficient IGM conditions that decompose the joint action-value function into individual components <cit.>. These decomposition strategies, however, impose structural constraints that limit the expressiveness of the joint action-value function classes they can model. Wang et al. highlight that such restricted function classes can cause suboptimal performance or unbounded divergence during off-policy training <cit.>. QTRAN addresses this limitation by offering a factorization framework that spans the complete value function space defined by IGM consistency, yet its exact implementation is intractable, and approximate versions exhibit instability and poor performance in complex environments <cit.>. Consequently, developing scalable methods for cooperative MARL remains an unresolved challenge.

In order to adapt the offloading strategies for dynamic scenarios, over recent years, DRL has been widely applied to solve task offloading problems in MEC systems. Dinh et al. <cit.> focused on the multi-user multi-edge-node computation offloading problem by using deep Q-learning. Chen et al. <cit.> considered an ultra-dense network, where multiple base stations can be selected for offloading. They also adopted deep Q-learning to obtain the offloading strategy. Huang et al. <cit.> proposed a DRL-based offloading framework which jointly considers both the offloading decisions and resource allocations. Zhan et al. <cit.> proposed an efficient task offloading method combining PPO and convolutional neural networks. Tan et al. <cit.> proposed a deep Q-learning based offloading method considering constraints of limited resources, vehicle's mobility and delay. Huang et al. <cit.> proposed a DRL-based online offloading framework to maximize the weighted sum of the computation rates of all the UE. Ning et al. <cit.> proposed a deep Q-learning based method for jointly optimising task offloading and resource allocation in MEC. The existing studies mostly assume the offloading problem as one learning task and apply conventional DRL algorithms to solve the task. However, many DRL algorithms suffer from poor sample efficiency — when facing new scenarios, those DRL-based offloading methods need long training time to find the effective policy, which impedes their practical deployment. To address this issue, our offloading method adopts an MRL approach which can efficiently solve new learning tasks with the requirement of only few gradient update steps and a small amount of data. As a result, our method can quickly adapt to the changes of environments with the requirement of only few training steps rather than fully retraining the offloading policy from scratch. With the low demands of computation and data, our method can efficiently run on the resource-constrained UE using its own data.
new_text:
In recent years, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a critical tool for adapting task offloading strategies in dynamic mobile edge computing (MEC) environments. Researchers have increasingly explored DRL to address challenges such as user mobility, resource limitations, and varying network conditions. For example, Dinh et al. focused on the multi-user, multi-edge-node offloading problem by leveraging deep Q-learning (DQL), a foundational DRL method. This approach aimed to optimize task allocation decisions across distributed edge resources. Chen et al. extended this work by modeling an ultra-dense network scenario, where multiple base stations are available for offloading, and similarly employed DQL to derive efficient strategies. Huang et al. proposed a more integrated solution by designing a DRL-based framework that simultaneously optimizes offloading decisions and resource allocation, addressing the interdependence between these factors. Meanwhile, Zhan et al. introduced a novel method combining proximal policy optimization (PPO), a policy gradient algorithm, with convolutional neural networks to enhance task offloading in complex environments. Tan et al. adapted DQL to incorporate constraints such as limited resources, vehicular mobility, and latency requirements, reflecting real-world operational challenges. Another contribution by Huang et al. centered on an online DRL framework designed to maximize the weighted sum of computation rates for all user equipment (UE). Ning et al. further advanced the field by jointly optimizing task offloading and resource allocation through DQL, demonstrating how resource contention can be managed more effectively.  

Despite these advancements, most existing methods treat the offloading problem as a single, static learning task using conventional DRL algorithms. However, this approach faces a significant limitation: poor sample efficiency. Conventional DRL algorithms typically require extensive training to converge on effective policies, and when new scenarios emerge (e.g., changes in network topology or user behavior), these models must be retrained from scratch, incurring substantial time and data costs. This inefficiency hinders the practical deployment of DRL-based offloading in rapidly evolving MEC environments. To overcome this, our proposed method leverages meta-reinforcement learning (MRL), a paradigm that enables rapid adaptation to new tasks with minimal training. By structuring the learning process to learn *how to learn* from past experiences, our approach requires only a few gradient update steps and a small amount of data to adjust to environmental changes. This significantly reduces the computational burden and eliminates the need for full retraining, making the solution viable for resource-constrained UEs that operate under stringent energy and processing limitations.

Inspired by the recent success of Transformer models in machine translation, we propose a new fusion method, TransModality, to address the task of multimodal sentiment analysis. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved strong performance in various applications.
    In the real world, network data is usually formed in a streaming fashion. The distributions of patterns that refer to neighborhood information of nodes may shift over time. The GNN model needs to learn the new patterns that cannot yet be captured. But learning incrementally leads to the catastrophic forgetting problem that historical knowledge is overwritten by newly learned knowledge. Therefore, it is important to train GNN model to learn new patterns and maintain existing patterns simultaneously, which few works focus on.
    In this paper, we propose a streaming GNN model based on continual learning so that the model is trained incrementally and up-to-date node representations can be obtained at each time step.
    Firstly, we design an approximation algorithm to detect new coming patterns efficiently based on information propagation. Secondly, we combine two perspectives of data replaying and model regularization for existing pattern consolidation. Specially, a hierarchy-importance sampling strategy for nodes is designed and a weighted regularization term for GNN parameters is derived, achieving greater stability and generalization of knowledge consolidation.
    Our model is evaluated on real and synthetic data sets and compared with multiple baselines. The results of node classification prove that our model can efficiently update model parameters and achieve comparable performance to model retraining. In addition, we also conduct a case study on the synthetic data, and carry out some specific analysis for each part of our model, illustrating its ability to learn new knowledge and maintain existing knowledge from different perspectives.
new_text: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved strong performance in various applications. Network data is often streaming, with node neighborhood pattern distributions shifting over time. GNNs must learn evolving patterns incrementally, but this risks catastrophic forgetting—overwriting historical knowledge with newly learned knowledge. Thus, training GNNs to learn new patterns while maintaining existing ones is critical, though few works address this. In this paper, we propose a streaming GNN model using continual learning to incrementally train and generate up-to-date node representations at each time step. We first design an efficient approximation algorithm for detecting newly arriving patterns via information propagation. We then combine data replaying and model regularization for consolidating existing patterns: a node hierarchy-importance sampling strategy is introduced, along with a weighted regularization term for GNN parameters to enhance knowledge consolidation stability and generalization. Evaluations on real and synthetic datasets, compared with multiple baselines, show node classification results demonstrate efficient parameter updates and performance comparable to retraining. A synthetic data case study with detailed component analysis further illustrates the model’s capacity to learn new knowledge and retain existing knowledge from multiple perspectives.

Naturally, we raise a question: given a pre-trained model, which dimension should we prune to minimize the model's accuracy loss? In practice, users empirically choose the most redundant dimension to prune, which often leads to a sub-optimal pruned model because of an inappropriate dimension choice. Worse, excessive pruning of any of these three dimensions will lead to unacceptable loss, as shown in Fig. <ref>. Instead, comprehensively pruning these dimensions yields better results. However, there has not been any effective method to achieve this. Though some previous methods can reduce the depth and width of the model simultaneously, the same methods are not applicable when considering image resolution[Please see Background and Related Works for the reason]. Motivated by <cit.>, the optimal values for these dimensions can also be observed in a brute-force manner, i.e., grid search. However, grid search is costly (over 500 GPU[GTX 1080Ti] hours for pruning ResNet for CIFAR-10) and often sub-optimal (if grid size > 1).
new_text: A key question emerges: for a given pre-trained model, which dimension should be pruned to minimize accuracy degradation? In practice, users often heuristically select the most redundant dimension, a strategy that frequently results in sub-optimal pruned models due to inadequate dimension selection. Furthermore, over-pruning any of these dimensions—whether depth, width, or spatial resolution—can cause significant performance degradation, as demonstrated in Fig. <ref>. While joint pruning across these dimensions improves outcomes, no efficient method currently achieves this effectively. Existing approaches that simultaneously prune depth and width are incompatible with spatial resolution reduction [Background and Related Works]. Although brute-force grid search, inspired by <cit.>, can identify optimal pruning ratios, it is computationally expensive (exceeding 500 GPU [GTX 1080Ti] hours for ResNet on CIFAR-10) and often fails to converge to global optima when the grid interval exceeds 1.

Pointwise operators are naturally dual-mode layers. Neural network layers that connect input and output neurons within each timestep (no across-connections among different timesteps) are often referred as pointwise operators <cit.>, including feed-forward layers (a.k.a., fully-connected layers or 1×1 convolution layers), activation layers (e.g., ReLU, Swish <cit.>), residual and dense connections <cit.>, striding layers, dropout layers <cit.> and element-wise multiplications. new_text: Pointwise operators inherently function as dual-mode components due to their architecture. Neural network layers that establish connections between input and output neurons within individual timesteps—without any connections across different timesteps—are typically classified as pointwise operators <cit.>. These include fully-connected layers (or 1×1 convolutional layers), activation functions (e.g., ReLU, Swish <cit.>), residual/dense connections <cit.>, striding mechanisms, dropout layers <cit.>, and element-wise operations. Since these layers do not facilitate temporal information propagation, they are inherently compatible with dual-mode structures and can be directly implemented in Universal ASR encoder architectures.
