In this paper, we bridge the gap between current multi-view 3D reconstruction and physically-based
differentiable rendering, and demonstrate high-quality reconstructions at competitive runtime performance.
We attack the challenging case of extracting explicit triangle meshes, PBR materials and environment
lighting from a set of multi-view images, in a format directly compatible with current DCC tools and game engines.
For improved visual fidelity, we compute direct illumination using Monte Carlo integration with ray tracing,
and add several techniques to combat the increased noise levels. By carefully trading variance for bias,
we enable efficient gradient-based optimization in a physically-based inverse rendering pipeline.
Compared to previous 3D reconstruction methods, our formulation primarily improves material and light separation.
new_text: This work establishes a connection between existing multi-view 3D reconstruction techniques and physically-based differentiable rendering, showcasing high-quality reconstructions with comparable runtime efficiency. We tackle the complex problem of generating explicit triangle meshes, physically-based rendering (PBR) materials, and environment lighting from multi-view image sets, ensuring compatibility with mainstream digital content creation (DCC) tools and game engines. To enhance visual accuracy, direct illumination is computed via Monte Carlo integration combined with ray tracing, alongside strategies to mitigate elevated noise levels. Through strategic variance-bias trade-offs, we facilitate efficient gradient-based optimization within a physically-based inverse rendering framework. Relative to prior 3D reconstruction approaches, our method markedly improves the separation of material properties and lighting conditions.

The ML research community have embraced DP as the gold standard for privacy protection. Yet, none of the related works in the literature employs the original formulation of DP, but relaxations of it, such as (ϵ,δ)-DP and others. On top of that, the privacy parameters used are quite far from what is considered theoretically “safe” (i.e., ϵ≤ 1 and negligible δ w.r.t. the population size). For such loose implementations, the
privacy guarantees of DP do not hold, and what is done can only be viewed as old plain noise addition, which at best provides ex post protection depending on the amount of noise added for a given ϵ, rather than on the ϵ value itself. This renders it rather pointless to claim use of the DP privacy model and comes close to the (often criticized) utility-first paradigm used in SDC for decades. Thus, the use of the “differential privacy” label by a lot of works whose implementations offer an actual privacy very far from truly sound DP can only be regarded as deceptive. To aggravate the matter, most of those works systematically omit empirical privacy analyses, because they consider any relaxation and parameterization of DP to be privacy-preserving enough.
new_text: The ML research community has adopted DP as the gold standard for privacy protection. However, no work in the literature uses the original DP formulation, instead relying on relaxations like (ε,δ)-DP and others. The privacy parameters employed are far from the theoretically “safe” thresholds (i.e., ε ≤ 1 and negligible δ w.r.t. population size), rendering DP guarantees invalid. Such implementations amount to traditional noise addition, offering at best ex post protection dependent on noise magnitude for a given ε, not ε itself. This undermines DP claims and aligns with the (often criticized) utility-first paradigm in SDC, as the actual privacy provided deviates significantly from rigorous DP. Further, most of these works systematically omit empirical privacy analyses, since they consider any relaxation of DP sufficient for privacy.

new_text: This study investigates the resilience of deep learning architectures against watermark shortcuts in chest X-ray (CXR) datasets. new_text: A fundamental principle underlying integrated gradients is “implementation invariance,” which requires that networks with equivalent functionality yield identical attribution results <cit.>. Scaling up language models has been shown to predictably improve performance and sample efficiency on a wide range of downstream tasks.
This paper instead discusses an unpredictable phenomenon that we refer to as emergent abilities of large language models.
We consider an ability to be emergent if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger models.
Thus, emergent abilities cannot be predicted simply by extrapolating the performance of smaller models.
The existence of such emergence implies that additional scaling could further expand the range of capabilities of language models.
new_text: Scaling up language models has been shown to consistently improve performance and sample efficiency on a broad array of downstream tasks. This paper introduces an unanticipated phenomenon we term emergent abilities in large language models. We define an emergent ability as one that is absent in smaller-scale models but present in larger-scale models. Thus, emergent abilities cannot be predicted by merely extrapolating the performance of smaller-scale models. The existence of these emergent abilities suggests that additional scaling could further broaden the range of language model capabilities.

old_text: The original CXRs were corrupted by synthetic shortcuts by adding label-associated watermarks. A unique symbol was assigned to each of the five labels, and at train time, each image was selected to be corrupted by shortcut features with a probability of 0.9. If selected to be corrupted, the image was given “correct" shortcuts with a probability of 0.9, meaning all positive label symbols were watermarked onto the image. Otherwise (with a probability of 0.1), the corrupted image was given “incorrect" shortcuts and all negative label symbols were watermarked onto the image.
new_text: To simulate the presence of synthetic shortcut features in the original chest X-ray (CXR) images, researchers introduced label-associated watermarks that acted as artificial cues. Each of the five possible labels in the dataset was assigned a unique symbolic identifier. During training, every image had a 90% probability of being corrupted with these synthetic shortcut features. When an image was selected for corruption, it could either receive "correct" or "incorrect" shortcuts. Specifically, if a corrupted image received a "correct" shortcut (which occurred in 90% of cases), its true label’s corresponding symbol was applied as a watermark, reinforcing an accurate association between the image and its label. Conversely, in the remaining 10% of corrupted images, the shortcuts were considered "incorrect," meaning that symbols linked to all other (negative) labels were watermarked instead, creating misleading associations. This process aimed to challenge models by introducing biases that could either align with or contradict the true labels.

It is also important to consider the evaluation metrics used to measure emergent abilities <cit.>.
For instance, using exact string match as the evaluation metric for long-sequence targets may disguise compounding incremental improvements as emergence.
Similar logic may apply for multi-step or arithmetic reasoning problems, where models are only scored on whether they get the final answer to a multi-step problem correct, without any credit given to partially correct solutions.
However, the jump in final answer accuracy does not explain why the quality of intermediate steps suddenly emerges to above random, and using evaluation metrics that do not give partial credit are at best an incomplete explanation, because emergent abilities are still observed on many classification tasks (e.g., the tasks in <ref>D–H).
new_text: The evaluation metrics used to assess emergent abilities <cit.> critically influence their perceived emergence. For example, relying on exact string matching for long-sequence targets risks obscuring gradual improvements as abrupt emergent behavior. A similar issue arises in multi-step or arithmetic reasoning tasks, where models receive credit solely for correct final answers, regardless of intermediate step accuracy. This creates a disconnect: while final answer accuracy improves sharply with scale, the sudden emergence of high-quality intermediate reasoning remains unexplained. Evaluation metrics that ignore partial correctness offer at best an incomplete account, since emergent abilities persist even in classification tasks (e.g., <ref>D–H), where such stepwise dependencies do not apply.

We analyzed the search behavior of ACG on a WideResNet-34-10 model trained by the method proposed in <cit.> using CIFAR-100, the only model in which the ASR of ACG was lower than that of APGD in the experiment using the CW loss (see <Ref>).
From <Ref>, it may be observed that the DI  of ACG of this model was lower than that of ACG on the other models.
This means that the search for ACG in this model tended to be more intensified than the attacks on the other two models <cit.>.
By contrast, the DI  of APGD on this model was higher than that of APGD in the other models, indicating that it tended to be more diversified.
These results suggest that the reason why APGD was superior to ACG for this model was because intensification was required to achieve a higher ASR.
However, the models requiring intensification for more effective attacks were rare because ACG exhibited a higher ASR than APGD for most of the models in <Ref>.
new_text: We analyzed the search behavior of ACG on a WideResNet-34-10 model trained using the method described in <cit.> on the CIFAR-100 dataset, the only model in which ACG’s ASR was lower than APGD’s ASR in the CW loss-based experiment (see <Ref>). Observations from <Ref> indicate that the Diversification Index (DI) of ACG for this model was lower compared to ACG’s DI on other models. This suggests that ACG’s search process for this specific model was more focused or "intensified"—prioritizing a narrower range of attack strategies—relative to its behavior on other models <cit.>. Conversely, APGD exhibited a higher DI on this model than on others, implying its attack strategies were more "diversified" here. These contrasting patterns point to a critical distinction: for this model, the lower ASR of ACG compared to APGD likely arose because the attack required a greater degree of intensification to overcome the model’s defenses. However, such a scenario was uncommon. In most models tested in <Ref>, ACG outperformed APGD in terms of ASR, suggesting these models did not demand the same level of intensification. In our study all models are pre-trained on ImageNet (upstream dataset) and then fine-tuned on downstream data. In this section, we explore if upstream robustness propagates downstream.

new_text:
Robustness to upstream dataset shifts  
In our study, all models are pre-trained on ImageNet (an upstream dataset) and then fine-tuned on downstream data. In this section, we explore whether upstream robustness transfers downstream. First, we observe in <ref> (left) that the original performance on ImageNet is linked to out-of-distribution (OOD) classification error in accordance with previous studies <cit.>. When adjusted for in-distribution (ID) classification error, clean ImageNet performance emerges as one of the strongest predictors of OOD classification error. Second, we find that robustness to ImageNet shifts provides little additional information about downstream robustness compared to clean performance. The performance on ImageNet shifts is nearly perfectly correlated with ID performance (in this setting, accuracy falls precisely on the line; c.f., <ref>), but this relationship does not generalize to our diverse set of downstream shifts.

The model is transferred using a set of (potentially few) examples from a new distribution. At test time, we assume that the classes remain the same (closed-world setting), but that the distribution may otherwise change. We specifically focus on the effect of distribution shifts after a model has been transferred to a new distribution (i.e., the downstream implications) and discuss the empirical differences and similarities compared to results concerning upstream OOD robustness that were discussed in previous studies <cit.>.
new_text: We follow the standard workflow for applying computer vision models to downstream tasks—particularly long-tail problems—by building on pre-trained backbones. Model transfer is performed using a limited set of examples from a new data distribution. At inference time, we assume class labels remain consistent with the training set (closed-world setting), while other distributional aspects may vary. Our analysis specifically targets distribution shifts that occur after model transfer (i.e., downstream implications) and systematically evaluates empirical patterns, contrasting these findings with upstream out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness results from prior studies <cit>.

Object detection, a dense prediction task characterized by complex network architectures comprising backbone, neck, and head components, forms the foundation of this study. We adopt Mask-RCNN <cit.> as the baseline model, replacing its backbone with ViT-B/L <cit.> pretrained using our proposed CSPT framework. The performance is evaluated on the publicly available remote sensing dataset DIOR <cit.>, which contains 23,463 images with 192,472 annotated instances across 20 object categories: airplane (AL), airport (AT), baseball field (BF), basketball court (BC), bridge (B), chimney (C), dam (D), expressway service area (ESA), expressway toll station (ETS), golf course (GC), ground track field (GTF), harbor (HB), overpass (O), ship (S), stadium (SD), storage tank (ST), tennis court (TC), train station (TS), vehicle (V), and windmill (W). Following DIOR’s data division protocol <cit.>, we benchmark our approach against state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods and advanced pretraining techniques. Classical detectors, including Faster-RCNN <cit.>, YOLOv5 <cit.>, Mask-RCNN <cit.>, PANet <cit.>, and CenterNet <cit.>, are selected for comparison, alongside RSD-specific SOTA models such as MSFC-Net <cit.>, CANet <cit.>, and FSoD <cit.>.  

As shown in the 9th and 14th rows of Table 6, our method outperforms the baseline Mask-RCNN <cit.> by 3% mAP using ViT-B <cit.> as the backbone, without requiring additional architectural modifications. Furthermore, with ViT-L <cit.> as the backbone—deployed in its standard configuration—we achieve 71.7% mAP, a result competitive with and in some cases superior to existing SOTA methods.  

Additionally, self-supervised pretraining approaches (e.g., MAE <cit.>, MoCo <cit.>, and SimMIM <cit.>) are compared in rows 9 to 12 of Table 6, each integrated as a backbone within Mask-RCNN <cit.>. These comparisons demonstrate that CSPT enables Mask-RCNN to achieve the highest performance among the tested pretraining strategies.

The IoU-based metric. The IoU-based trajectory metric is computed as follows: given two predicted trajectory sets (with and without perturabtion), we first upsample all predicted trajectories (6 of them in each set) to 100Hz, and then voxelize them into a 2D top down grid with resolution of 0.5 meters. We then count the number of voxels both sets occupy, divided by the total number of voxels either output set occupies. To simplify computation, we explicitly ignore the probabilities and speeds of trajectories. This measure quantifies "how geometrically different the trajectories look". An IoU of 1 means the trajectories did not meaningfully change, and an IoU of 0 means the trajectories do not overlap at all. While more complicated versions of this metric could be computed (e.g. earth movers distance), we found this metric intuitive and useful for finding interesting shifts due to perturbation.
new_text: The IoU-based trajectory metric is computed as follows: given two predicted trajectory sets (with and without perturbation), we first upsample all predicted trajectories (six in each set) to 100 Hz, then voxelize them into a 2D top-down grid at a resolution of 0.5 meters. We calculate the IoU by dividing the count of voxels shared by both sets by the total count of voxels occupied by either set. To simplify computation, we explicitly disregard trajectory probabilities and speeds. This measure quantifies how geometrically distinct the trajectories appear. An IoU of 1 indicates the trajectories underwent no meaningful changes, while an IoU of 0 indicates no overlap. While more complex variants of this metric could be computed (e.g., Earth Mover’s Distance), we found this version intuitive and effective for identifying significant shifts caused by perturbation.

In this paper, we propose Point-McBert, a Bert-style pre-training method for point cloud pre-training, which tackle the problem of improper tokenizer in previous work.
We release the previous strict single-choice constraint on patches and utilize the probability distribution vector of token ids as supervision signals to avoid semantically-similar patches corresponding to different token ids.
In addition, we use the high-level semantics generated by transformer to refine the probability distribution vector to further avoid semantically-dissimilar patches corresponding to the same token ids.
Extensive experiments on different datasets and downstream tasks are conducted to evaluate the performance of our Point-McBert.
The results show that our Point-McBert not only improves the performance of previous work on all downstream tasks with almost no extra computational overhead, but also achieve new state-of-the-art on point cloud classification and point cloud few-shot learning.
The experiments also reveal that our pre-training method successfully transfer knowledge learned from unlabeled data to downstream tasks, which has great potential in point cloud learning.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were recently proposed for the session-based recommendation task. The models showed promising improvements over traditional recommendation approaches.
In this work, we further study RNN-based models for session-based recommendations.
We propose the application of two techniques to improve model performance, namely, data augmentation, and a method to account for shifts in the input data distribution.
We also empirically study the use of generalised distillation, and a novel alternative model that directly predicts item embeddings.
Experiments on the RecSys Challenge 2015 dataset demonstrate relative improvements of 12.8% and 14.8% over previously reported results on the Recall@20 and Mean Reciprocal Rank@20 metrics respectively.
new_text: Recent studies have introduced RNNs for session-based recommendation tasks, with these models demonstrating significant performance enhancements compared to conventional recommendation systems. Building on these findings, this research extends the investigation of RNN-based models within session-based recommendation systems. Two strategies are introduced to enhance model effectiveness: data augmentation techniques and a method addressing changes in the input data distribution. Additionally, the study explores generalized distillation and a novel model variant that directly predicts item embeddings. Experimental results using the RecSys Challenge 2015 dataset show relative performance gains of 12.8% in Recall@20 and 14.8% in Mean Reciprocal Rank@20 compared to prior studies.

old_text: Users of e-commerce websites are often inundated by the huge number of items available for sale. Recommender systems can be used to enhance user experience by making personalized and useful recommendations for each user. For example, the system could automatically display items of interest, or suggest new discounts relevant to each user. In order to personalize recommendations, traditional recommender systems often need to build up a user profile. Collaborative filtering approaches <cit.> can define user-user similarity based on their history of purchases, or they could rely on matrix factorization to build latent factor vectors for each user. Crucially, these approaches require the user to be identified when making recommendations. This may not always be possible: new users to the site will not have any profile, or users may not be logged in, or they may have deleted their tracking information. This leads to the problem of cold-start for recommendation methods that require user history.
new_text: Users of e-commerce websites are often inundated by the vast selection of products available for purchase. To address this, recommender systems enhance user experience by offering personalized and useful recommendations. These systems might, for example, automatically highlight items of interest or promote new discounts tailored to individual preferences. Traditional recommendation approaches typically require constructing user profiles to enable personalization. Collaborative filtering methods can define user-user similarity based on purchase histories or employ matrix factorization to generate latent factor vectors for users. Crucially, these strategies necessitate identifying users at the time of recommendation. However, this requirement presents challenges: new users may lack profiles, users might not be logged in, or tracking data could have been deleted. These scenarios highlight the limitations of user-history-dependent methods, ultimately leading to the cold-start problem.

The reasons of the significant increase in the KV store sizes of HyperLevelDB
and PebblesDB are two-fold. First, both HyperLevelDB and PebblesDB compact
only selected ranges of keys to reduce write amplification. Specifically,
HyperLevelDB selects the largest range of keys in the upper level that covers
the smallest range of keys in the lower level to perform compaction, and
places a limit on the total volume of KV pairs in each compaction. This
reduces the amount of invalid KV pairs being reclaimed from the lower level
during compaction. PebblesDB divides keys in each level into disjoint ranges
and compacts each range only when its size reaches a predefined threshold. To
enable fast compaction, PebblesDB only partitions KV pairs in the selected
ranges and directly inserts them into the lower level, without removing
invalid KV pairs in the lower level. This also reduces the amount of invalid
KV pairs being reclaimed.
new_text: The significant increase in KV store sizes in HyperLevelDB and PebblesDB stems from their compaction strategies aimed at reducing write amplification. HyperLevelDB compacts only selected key ranges by choosing the largest overlapping range between upper and lower levels and limiting the total KV pairs per compaction. This minimizes invalid KV pairs reclaimed from lower levels. PebblesDB partitions each level into disjoint key ranges, compacting a range only when its size meets a threshold. To accelerate compaction, it inserts selected ranges directly into the lower level without removing invalid KVs, similarly reducing reclamation of invalid data. Both approaches curtail invalid KV pair retrieval during compaction.

new_text:
**Experiment 7 (Selective Key-Value (KV) Separation):**  
We assess the influence of selective KV separation on the update efficiency of `HashKV`. Three configurations of small-to-large KV ratios are tested: 1:2, 1:1, and 2:1. Small KV pairs are defined as 40 B, while large KV pairs are either 1 KiB or 4 KiB. With the selective KV separation threshold set to 192 B (<ref>), small KV pairs are stored in their entirety within the LSM-tree, whereas large KV pairs are managed through separation. Figure <ref> presents performance comparisons with and without selective KV separation. Enabling this technique boosts throughput by 23.2–118.0% for 1 KiB large KVs and 19.2–52.1% for 4 KiB large KVs. Higher gains are observed in workloads with a larger proportion of small KVs, owing to the elevated overhead of updating small KVs under separation. Additionally, selective KV separation reduces total write sizes by 14.1–39.6% for 1 KiB large KVs and 4.1–10.7% for 4 KiB large KVs.

We propose a novel sparse spectrum approximation of Gaussian process
(GP) tailored for Bayesian optimisation. Whilst the current sparse
spectrum methods provide good approximations for regression problems,
it is observed that this particular form of sparse approximations
generates an overconfident GP, i.e. it predicts less variance than
the original GP. Since the balance between predictive mean and the
predictive variance is a key determinant in the success of Bayesian
optimisation, the current sparse spectrum methods are less suitable.
We derive a regularised marginal likelihood for finding the optimal
frequencies in optimisation problems. The regulariser trades the accuracy
in the model fitting with targeted increase in the variance of the
resultant GP. We first consider the entropy of the distribution over
the maxima as the regulariser that needs to be maximised. Later we
show that the Expected Improvement acquisition function can also be
used as a proxy for that, thus making the optimisation less computationally
expensive. Experiments show an increase in the Bayesian optimisation
convergence rate over the vanilla sparse spectrum method.
new_text: We propose a novel sparse spectrum approximation method for Gaussian processes (GPs) specifically designed for Bayesian optimisation (BO). While existing sparse spectrum techniques effectively approximate GPs in regression tasks, they tend to produce an overconfident model that underestimates predictive variance compared to the original GP. This issue arises because the sparse approximations prioritize fitting the mean response while discarding certain spectral components, which inadvertently reduces the model’s uncertainty estimates. In BO, however, the interplay between predictive mean and variance is critical for effective decision-making. An overconfident GP biases acquisition functions, leading to suboptimal exploration-exploitation trade-offs, and ultimately degrading the performance of BO algorithms. To address this, we introduce a regularised marginal likelihood framework that optimizes the selection of spectral frequencies. The regulariser introduces a controlled trade-off between fitting the data and explicitly increasing the predictive variance of the resulting GP. Initially, we formalize the regulariser as the entropy of the distribution over potential maxima, ensuring that the model maintains a diverse set of plausible optimal regions. This entropy-based approach, however, can be computationally demanding. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition function—already central to BO—can serve as a computationally efficient proxy for this entropy maximisation. By leveraging EI during the regularisation process, we maintain the variance-increasing benefits of the entropy objective while reducing computational overhead. Empirical results confirm that this method accelerates the convergence of Bayesian optimisation compared to the standard sparse spectrum approach, without compromising model accuracy.

Actually, cut deletion or clean-up strategies are important when multiple cuts are added to the master problems at each iteration <cit.>. Most existing works use mathematical methods to develop cut clean-up strategies. A similar work that has leveraged ML techniques to develop cut clean-up strategies can be found in <cit.>, where the authors have accelerated Benders decomposition <cit.> especially for the two-stage stochastic programming problems. Specifically, the authors have used ML techniques to evaluate cuts and their proposed method is instance-specific, which means a specific model is needed for each instance and the training process is conducted online. new_text: Cut deletion or clean-up strategies become critical in optimization frameworks when multiple cuts are iteratively added to the master problem. This necessity arises because excessive or redundant cuts can hinder solver efficiency or slow convergence. While most prior research relies on mathematical criteria—such as angle-based or distance-based metrics—to design clean-up strategies, a recent study <cit.> has explored machine learning (ML) as an alternative for accelerating Benders decomposition in two-stage stochastic programming. The authors trained ML models to evaluate and select informative cuts, aiming to reduce computational overhead. However, their approach is instance-specific: a separate model must be trained for each problem instance, with the training conducted online (during the solving process). This contrasts with typical requirements in wireless network optimization, where pre-trained, generalizable models and offline training are preferred for scalability and deployment efficiency. Furthermore, two-stage stochastic programming problems differ fundamentally from mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problems commonly encountered in wireless resource allocation. Generalized Benders Decomposition (GBD) in MINLP generates cuts that are structurally more complex and harder to characterize than those in Benders decomposition, complicating direct adaptation of the ML strategy. Consequently, the methods in <cit.> cannot be straightforwardly applied to wireless scenarios without significant modifications to address these differences in problem structure and cut behavior.

To the best of our knowledge, it has not been proven that deciding the existence of a valid itinerary for the unlabeled version (assuming T is stationary, and allowing one move per disc) is NP-hard, but similar reconfiguration problems, such as those called OMC <cit.> and U-TRANS-RP <cit.>, have been shown to be NP-hard.
Both problems seek to find a valid itinerary of translations of discs from a start configuration to a target configuration.
Specifically, in OMC (one move per coin), each of the discs is given a subset of possible final targets, and can move (as in our model) exactly once.
In U-TRANS-RP, the goal is to decide whether a valid itinerary of at most k moves exists, for the unlabeled variant.
The NP-hardness of U-TRANS-RP is shown for the case where k is smaller than n (some discs are already at the target locations, and some may move more than once).

new_text: To the best of our knowledge, it has not been formally established whether determining the existence of a valid itinerary for the unlabeled version—where the translation model assumes a stationary target configuration *T* and permits exactly one move per disc—is NP-hard. However, related reconfiguration problems with analogous constraints have been proven to be NP-hard, providing a benchmark for reasoning about computational complexity in similar contexts. For example, the One Move per Coin (OMC) problem involves determining if a set of unlabeled discs can be moved in a single step from an initial configuration to a target configuration, where each disc has a predefined subset of possible final positions. This aligns with the model considered here, as each disc is allowed to move exactly once under the same translation rules. Similarly, the U-TRANS-RP problem focuses on deciding whether an unlabeled reconfiguration can be achieved using at most *k* moves. Crucially, this variant is proven NP-hard when *k* is less than the total number of discs *n*, which implies that some discs must already be at their target locations, while others may require multiple moves. These results suggest that reconfiguration problems with move constraints share intrinsic computational challenges, even when the specific details of the problem instances differ. While no formal reduction has yet been established from OMC or U-TRANS-RP to our unlabeled setting, the structural similarities between these problems lead us to conjecture that the unlabeled version of our model is also NP-hard. Consequently, optimizing for certain criteria—such as minimizing the total displacement in the SA-UST(*S*,*T*) framework—would likely inherit or even amplify the computational difficulty, making it likely NP-hard as well.

new_text: Spatial blockages are categorized as static (e.g., buildings and immobile fixtures), dynamic (e.g., humans and moving obstructions), and self-blockages (e.g., self-hand blocking). Static blockage impacts are traditionally modeled via shadowing <cit.>, while stochastic models characterize statistics of dynamic and self-blockages <cit.>. To address channel uncertainties from random blockages, robust beamforming strategies have been proposed <cit.>. Blockage probability learning through spatiotemporal image sensing side information <cit.> enabled worst-case robust beamforming in CoMP systems, considering all blockage pattern combinations <cit.>. However, the ergodic method’s high computational complexity prompted outage-minimum strategies using stochastic optimization for CoMP <cit.>. Deploying multiple BSs in CoMP leverages spatial diversity to compensate for blockage-induced performance loss but incurs high hardware and power costs. An alternative cost-efficient solution <cit.> involves reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs), creating alternative communication links via RIS-assisted mmWave systems.

If Δ t < 0, the new packets from ⟨ f,p' ⟩ arrive too early.

new_text: When the time difference Δ t between consecutive packet batches is positive (Δ t > 0), it introduces a measurable delay between the final packet of the sequence ⟨ f,p ⟩ and the initial packet of the subsequent sequence ⟨ f,p' ⟩. Conversely, if Δ t is negative (Δ t < 0), the packets from ⟨ f,p' ⟩ arrive at the network before the final packets of ⟨ f,p ⟩ have been fully transmitted, creating a temporal misalignment. This misalignment can result in packets from ⟨ f,p' ⟩ overtaking packets from ⟨ f,p ⟩ if the system allows end-to-end deadlines to exceed the defined cycle time (t_cycle). Such overtaking disrupts the expected transmission order, as packets are processed based on arrival time rather than sequence order. To quantify this effect, the number of packets that arrive out of their original order and lack a guaranteed inter-arrival time of t_cycle can be bounded. This upper bound is calculated as n_transition ≤ 2·⌈|Δ t|/t_cycle⌉, where the ceiling function accounts for discrete cycle time intervals and the factor of 2 accommodates both early and delayed packets in the worst-case scenario.

the VP's runtime environment. This means our device customization is invisible to VP's user-mode apps.
Although our user-level device virtualization allows the VP's process to share certain services in the host system,
with the `device` namespace isolation, a user-mode app running in the VP is still unaware of device-specific differences.
Second, our VP's customization does not interfere with normal operations on the host device.
System modifications without leveraging OS-level virtualization lack flexibility and compatibility.
Besides, they are very difficult to achieve the same transparent and stealthy capability as VPDroid,
as blindly changing return values of APIs/syscalls is likely to cause system crashes or exceptions (e.g., Bluetooth system services keep restarting).
Due to the multiplexing of hardware devices, VPDroid avoids incompatibility issues by
decoupling device-attribute editing operations from normal operations on the host device.
